b: Topographic effffects such as varying illumination and shadowing introduce substantial distortions in surface reflflectance estimation. These distortions manifest as overestimated reflflectance in sunlit areas and underestimated values in shadowed regions [1]. Known as Terrain Correction (TC) methods, physically based and semi empirical approaches are proposed to mitigate these issues. Regarding semi empirical approaches, there are for instance C correction and C SE correction [2], A major drawback of these approaches is a critical dependency with terrain and environmental conditions.

To overcome this situation, in [3], an optimal estimation algorithm [4] is used to retrieve surface geometry directly from the spectral information. For this purpose, all parameters involved into an unifified atmospheric– topographic correction model are estimated starting from prior values (Statistical Bayesian inference). It leads in particular to refifinement of digital elevation model parameters.

The objective of this poster is to present our implementation of this optimal estimation method. Data preparation steps are discussed. These are dealing with the generation of radiative transfer dataset by using CAMS data [5] and 6S [6], the collection of surface reflflectance signature [7], the retrievals of topographic information by using COPDEM [5] and VHR DEM. The second part of this poster is dedicated to the physical and the mathematical models involved into this processing, respectively the formulation of forward model with a radiance equation (tailored for TC) and the Optimal Estimation (OE) formulation. Finally, results obtained by using PRISMA hyperspectral dataset observed over Grande Canaria island landscape are report.

For completeness, as this framework involved many components, our intermediate results (from radiative transfer code parametrization, PRISMA pre processing, Spectral analysis, OE set up with correct uncertainties) are discussed.

b: Accurate geolocation is a fundamental requirement for the geometric quality, interoperability, and scientific usability of Earth Observation (EO) products. Global reference datasets such as the Copernicus Sentinel-2 Global Reference Image (GRI) provide a consistent basis for georeferencing enhancement and geometric calibration or validation; however, their spatial resolution is substantially lower than national geospatial datasets available in many European countries. Open national orthophotomap datasets therefore represents a potentially valuable complementary source of reference information for EO geolocation assessment and refinement.

This study evaluates the suitability of openly available Polish national orthophotography as a reference dataset for EO image geolocation and compares its performance with the Sentinel-2 GRI. The Polish orthophotomap is commonly available at 25 cm ground sampling distance (GSD), with resolutions of 10 cm or better in urban areas and locally reaching 3 cm, representing an increase in spatial sampling of approximately 40 to over 300 times relative to the 10 m GRI. This substantially higher spatial detail enables more precise identification of stable features, that can support geometric quality assessment.

In this work, Polish open orthophotomap dataset is evaluated as a reference source for improving the geolocation of satellite imagery and compared with the GRI-based approach. A proprietary image-matching and geometric refinement workflow is used, while the contribution focuses on the influence of the reference dataset itself rather than on the internal processing methodology. The analysis quantifies the initial and corrected positional errors and evaluates how reference-image resolution affects the achievable geolocation accuracy.

The study also highlights a broader opportunity: many European countries maintain high-resolution authoritative orthophotomaps, but access conditions, formats and metadata remain fragmented. These findings expose the potential value of a harmonized European catalogue of open reference imagery and geospatial datasets specifically designed to support georeferencing enhancement and geometric quality assessment.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Cédric Traizet<sup>1</sup>, Antoine Martinez<sup>1</sup>, Emmanuel Hillairet<sup>1</sup>, Antoine Burie<sup>1</sup>, Jonathan Guinet<sup>1</sup>
b: In September 2024, the Sentinel-2C (S2C) satellite was launched with the aim of replacing the Sentinel-2A (S2A) satellite. As S2A remains fully operational, a S2A extended campaign has been approved by ESA, and the S2A and Sentinel-2B (S2B) satellites were positioned in adjacent near-synchronous orbits with a 30-minute interval. This configuration offers a wide range of scientific opportunities to be explored. Notably, as the orbits are polar, the closer the satellite positions are to the poles, the closer they come to one another. This arrangement results in an overlap of swaths at mid and high latitudes. In this context, it is possible to obtain images of the same geographical location taken from two different viewing angles, offering the possibility of carrying out stereoscopic processing to generate elevation data. Moreover, the quasi-synchronous nature of S2A and S2B results in minimal variation in cloud cover and lighting conditions between acquisitions, which reduces the impact of clouds and shadows on the resulting products. This opportunity is further reinforced by ESA's on demand release of Level-1B sensor-geometry data, the data level required to perform stereoscopic reconstruction. L1B data consists of datastrips that represent all the data collected within the swath width of an S2 satellite over a defined period of time.

In this context, CS Group has undertaken work on this topic in order to demonstrate the feasibility of producing DSMs (Digital Surface Model) from pairs of Sentinel-2 (S2) images and to develop a tool enabling large-scale, frequently-updated DSM production at 10 meters resolution.

This presentation introduces the methodology used to achieve this objective. The open-source stereo pipeline CARS [1] and its geometric heart Shareloc [2] were used to perform the stereoscopic processing. To operate, CARS requires specific conditions, namely the use of sensor-geometry images accompanied by a compatible direct-location geometric model. In order to meet these requirements, the L1B sensor-geometry data provided by ESA were used to transform the geometric model of each granule into a generic and portable viewing model, structured as a multi-altitude (multi-H) sampled grid, using the open-source tool Sen2VM [3]. This methodology allows a pair of L1B granules to be seamlessly integrated into CARS, along with their associated geometric model, in order to produce a DSM. Scaling up the process requires management of L1B data tiling to automate DSM production over a large dataset. To validate the proposed methodology, the processing chain was executed on a selected set of study cases. A comprehensive evaluation with the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM, encompassing both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments, is presented in this study to benchmark the quality of the resulting stereo-derived DSMs.

b: Access to consistent, quality-controlled Earth Observation (EO) data remains a major barrier to the operational use of satellite information in data-scarce regions. We present Morocco Open Data Cube, a scalable, modular and open-source platform for the ingestion, querying, processing, visualization and analysis of large volumes of raw and Analysis Ready Data (ARD) over Morocco and, prospectively, the African continent. It operates in both archive and near-real-time modes. The Open Data Cube (ODC) geospatial data engine and the FastAPI web framework constitute the foundation of this Python-based platform. This platform provides a uniform and high-performance architecture, both in terms of data quantity and quality, and is scalable for managing multi-thematic geospatial and EO data.

This ARD technology is built on the Open Data Cube (ODC) geospatial data engine and the FastAPI web framework. This platform provides a uniform and high-performance architecture, both in terms of data quantity and quality, and is scalable for managing multi-thematic geospatial and EO data.

The solution was built using a range of good practices to construct geospatial data platforms: the ingestion pipeline, the query layer, and visual display interface are maintained as architecturally modular units so that each component can be updated or further developed independently; asynchronous task processing via Celery and Redis is used as the default implementation model for ARD retrieval functions, ensuring unblocked throughput under multiple concurrent requests; All products saved upon intake are standardized to CEOS-ARD standards, guaranteeing that the data is radiometrically calibrated, geometrically rectified, and spatially aligned before any further processing. For a more enhanced user experience, the platform uses external visualization engines like 3D volumetric exploration and MapX for EO storytelling as first-class interface components to connect operational data pipelines to user-friendly analytical tools that adhere to OGC standards. The platform includes a REST API as well as interactive documentation and workflow examples. This platform is projected as an extendable theme ecosystem, with modules such as urban planning and land-use/cover scenario modeling, urban hydrology and water footprint assessment, and a multi-hazard early warning system that incorporates land subsidence, flood, drought, and wildfire risk layers. Our primary scientific goal in developing this platform is to lower the technical barrier to satellite data access in data-scarce regional contexts while also providing a reproducible geospatial intelligence and EO infrastructure for sustainable development and climate resilience in Morocco and across the African continent.

b: Spire operates one of the world’s largest multi-purpose CubeSat constellations. A core capability is RF monitoring for environmental applications utilizing Spire’s proprietary L-band receiver, STRATOS. ESA’s Earthnet Data Assessment Pilot (EDAP) has evaluated STRATOS data and downstream products since 2020. Key deliverables, such as GNSS Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO) profile measurements, are now procured operationally by major numerical weather prediction (NWP) centers, namely NOAA and EUMETSAT, under strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs). Additionally, emerging R&D products are made available to the European research community via EarthNet and Third Party Mission (TPM) program to support pre-operational evaluation and scientific application.

In this presentation, we outline Spire’s approach to enabling community-driven Calibration and Validation (Cal/Val) across our diverse payload portfolio, demonstrating how high-volume commercial data streams are evaluated through scientific partnerships and operational impact studies. Some use cases include:

Atmospheric & Weather Applications: For Polarimetric RO (PRO), Spire provides novel precipitation-sensitive measurements, enabling independent validation and weather forecasting impact studies conducted by ESA and ECMWF.

Surface Remote Sensing: For GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R), community-led research on Spire's reflection data has yielded monthly Arctic sea ice thickness maps as well as ocean surface wind retrievals, with independent assimilation trials by ECMWF and the UK Met Office demonstrating positive forecasting impact.
Space Weather: Precise Orbit Determination (POD) data streams are made available to researchers to assess and model thermospheric and ionospheric dynamics.

Looking ahead, we present the roadmap for use of the novel hyperspectral microwave sounder (HyMS) data, a promising new water vapor sensor for NWP, and potential synergies with EDAP modeled on previous use cases. Finally, we show how this open-access research model extends to aviation tracking and RF monitoring, providing validated, multi-application datasets to support European security needs within the Copernicus Contributing Missions (CCM) framework.

b: Continuous radiometric calibration and validation underpin the scientific usability of any new Earth-observation constellation. The inter-calibration of the multispectral (MS HEO pathfinder) component of the Italian IRIDE constellation is being developed as a globally distributed effort, with reference matchups sought across sites worldwide; this contribution presents an early feasibility assessment of one specific question within that framework — whether high-latitude regions offer practical advantages as targets for inter-calibration. Polar regions are both scientifically critical, hosting the environmental and climatic processes that evolve most rapidly, and analytically demanding: conventional instrumented and pseudo-invariant calibration sites (PICS) are sparse there, while persistently large solar zenith angles place these acquisitions at the edge of standard calibration assumptions.

We assemble an initial set of spatio-temporally coincident matchups between IRIDE MS and well-characterised reference sensors. Sentinel -2 provides the primary reference, complemented by Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), whose wide swath offers favourable repeat coverage at high latitudes — an attractive property for the very question under study. Discovery and pairing are automated through a STAC-based pipeline spanning the IRIDE, Copernicus and EarthData catalogues (with VIIRS archives being integrated), and cloud screening is evaluated specifically on the IRIDE footprint. The matchups collected so far span two representative high-latitude settings — Dome C (Antarctica) and the Greenland ice sheet. In parallel, we are gathering matchups at mid-latitudes as well, to read the polar behaviour against a more conventional baseline and bring the differences into relief. Per-band gains are derived from the near-coincident acquisitions, using instrument spectral response functions, explicit treatment of spectral band-adjustment (SBAF) differences, and a GUM-compliant uncertainty budget.

These first results set the relevance of situates the high-latitude matchups within IRIDE's worldwide cross-calibration strategy and discusses, on the basis of this early evidence, to what extent high-latitude targets — ice sheets and polar PICS-like surfaces — are convenient and reliable for constellation-level inter-calibration, along with the geometric and atmospheric factors that condition their use.

This effort includes an integrating sphere with specially qualified QTH lamps, a diffuser panel and OGSE to support pre-launch calibration. b: NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) are advancing a new paradigm for Sustainable Land Imaging (SLI) that complements the enduring Landsat Program with emerging commercial capabilities. The SLI Commercial Transition Strategy seeks to first study the feasibility of establishing a resilient hybrid ecosystem that combines the strengths of public and private investments to deliver trusted, science-quality land information at greater scale, frequency, and diversity. Upon successful integration of public-private land products, the strategy will evolve into broad scale incorporation of harmonized surface reflectance and temperature products to support gold-standard science and critical applications. The short-term goal will enable augmentation of current government derived products with the long-term goal being the replacement of data and products from government-owned Landsat missions with equivalent data and products enabled by commercial satellite constellations in the 2030s.

This presentation will provide an overview of NASA and USGS’s evolving commercial transition strategy, including the transition from mission-centric architectures toward product- and application-driven approaches that leverage commercial innovation. It will highlight ongoing engagement with industry through the SLI Commercial Transition Plan, the role of calibration and validation in ensuring harmonization capability and scientific integrity, and opportunities for commercial providers to contribute across the value chain—from satellite data acquisition to advanced analytics and decision support.

This presentation will also discuss how NASA, USGS, industry, academia, and international partners can collectively accelerate innovation while preserving the long-term continuity, quality, and open accessibility that have made Landsat the global standard for land observations. Participants will gain insight into future partnership opportunities and the U.S. government vision for a sustainable, commercially enabled land imaging enterprise that expands the societal and economic impact of Earth observations for decades to come.

b: Labsphere, Inc. in conjunction with NASA GSFC and Genesis Engineering Solutions Inc., has developed an innovative, vacuum compatible, calibration spectro-radiometric illumination source with a highly uniform large-area rectangular flat panel active area. This device features a uniquely shaped diffuse integration geometry to achieve high uniformity over a large active output area while maintaining a smaller and more robust overall form-factor when compared to previous designs or integrating spheres. A new liquid-cooled hybrid quartz-tungsten (QT) and light emitting diode (LED) source module has been engineered to provide direct-in-vacuum reference illumination over the full dynamic range and spectrum of the VIIRS instrument’s optical bands during pre-launch testing. The first unit has been demonstrated to meet its requirements using ambient technology and a fully-vacuum-compatible second unit is planned to allow testing in thermal vacuum (TVAC) campaigns. This technology is flexible and capable of meeting the needs of many other instruments/missions requiring this type of test/calibration capability.

b: Railroad Valley is located in the Great Basin Desert region of the southwestern USA, with a size of approximately 130 km × 32 km. Railroad Valley Playa is a 15 km × 15 km dry lakebed situated within this region in east-central Nevada. Its remote location, arid high-desert climate, relatively vegetation-free and flat topography make it an ideal location for the ground-based radiometric calibration of airborne and spaceborne sensors. The Remote Sensing Group of the Wyant College of Optical Sciences at the University of Arizona has successfully used this site since 1996. Field deployments at other test sites such as White Sands Missile Range, Ivanpah Playa, and Lunar Lake were used to verify and authenticate the protocols for the atmospheric and surface reflectance measurements required in order to obtain the highest quality data for comparison with Earth-observation sensors. The on-site research was coupled with radiative transfer model integration to create a complete package used to determine the at-sensor spectral radiance (or reflectance) for sensors in the solar-reflective spectral range (400 nm to 2500 nm). The list of airborne and spaceborne sensors that the group has calibrated is too extensive to list here, but it includes national and international space programs as well as many commercial systems. The University of Arizona field work at Railroad Valley over the past thirty years has also resulted in two significant outcomes: the development of a historical data record of surface and atmospheric measurements at Railroad Valley, and expertise in the development of radiometric field instruments suitable for year-round continuous measurements in remote locations.

Coordinated efforts by national and international groups led to the concept and recommendation for automated and networked instrumented test sites. One of the outcomes of this concept is the Radiometric Calibration Network Working Group (RadCalNet WG), which is under the oversight of the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) Working Group on Calibration and Validation (WGCV) and the Infrared Visible Optical Sensors (IVOS). The Radiometric Calibration Test Site (RadCaTS) at Railroad Valley was developed by the University of Arizona in the early 2000s using the experience gained from prior in situ field work at Railroad Valley and other desert test sites. RadCaTS was initially used to supplement the reflectance-based approach, which was one of the traditional methods used by the group. Proof-of-concept prototype radiometers and the development of data processing algorithms occurred from 2002 to 2010. The outcome of this phase was weatherproof, solar-powered, multispectral ground-viewing radiometers (GVRs) that continue to provide measurements every two minutes throughout the day. Improvements in data telemetry over the past decade has allowed the group to reliably upload and process data on a daily basis, including web camera imagery. RadCaTS is one of original RadCalNet sites, and data are available from 2013 to present on the RadCalNet web portal (www.radcalnet.org).

The RadCaTS data provided to RadCalNet follow the standard temporal and spectral specifications: 09:00 to 15:00 (local standard time, every 30 minutes), 400 nm to 2500 nm (in 10 nm intervals), and a nadir view. Most sensors will observe the site with a different viewing geometry at a time that is not exactly on a 30 minute RadCalNet interval. This overview describes the RadCaTS processing method, an SI-traceable uncertainty analysis, and provides best practice suggestions for using the RVUS data, including current and emerging capabilities specific to RadCaTS.

b: Planet's Tanager-1 satellite provides imaging spectroscopy across the 380–2500 nm range with 5 nm spectral sampling. It is the first satellite in a planned constellation of space-based hyperspectral sensors supporting global methane and CO2 plume detection and mitigation through the Carbon Mapper Coalition. Tanager operates on a low-cost smallsat platform without onboard calibration hardware. As a result, achieving radiometric calibration that is accurate, stable, and traceable across sensors and over time depends on external reference-based methods. In Tanager's multi-sensor architecture, lunar calibration plays a key role in ensuring consistent, harmonized data products across the full constellation. Traditional vicarious calibration methods using desert playas and instrumented ground sites remain essential. However, they can be limited by atmospheric variability, surface anisotropy, and ground-instrument uncertainties.

The Moon is an ideal complementary reference. It is effectively invariant on decadal timescales, easy to observe on a frequent cadence, and its bidirectional reflectance and irradiance can be modeled at high spectral resolution. Since 2016, most of Planet's multi-spectral satellites have captured the Moon every month. Recent hyperspectral missions such as EnMAP have also highlighted the value of lunar observations for orbital imaging spectroscopy.

In this work, we present results from the first six months of regular lunar acquisitions collected by Tanager. Building on established lunar calibration models such as ROLO and LIME, we track absolute radiometric accuracy, temporal stability, and spectral response. We also highlight the utility of lunar observations for characterizing spatial sharpness, stray light performance, and subtle systematic noise structures in vicarious calibration coefficients derived from field campaigns.

As upcoming global imaging spectroscopy missions such as ESA's CHIME and NASA's EAGLE prepare to incorporate lunar calibration, Tanager serves as a practical pathfinder for cross-calibration and inter-mission data harmonization.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Eric Peters<sup>1</sup>, Saif Aati<sup>1</sup>
b: Tanager, first launched by Planet Labs in 2024, is a state-of-the-art imaging spectrometer for detecting high-emission point sources, particularly methane super-emitters. Robust association of repeated plume detections with a single methane source requires both high absolute geolocation accuracy and strong relative alignment across time. We present an operational ortho-rectification pipeline that calibrates a rigorous sensor model and jointly refines ancillary satellite telemetry parameters to produce sub-pixel Tanager imagery. Validation on 1,160 Tanager-1 scenes acquired in early 2026 demonstrates a rectification accuracy of 0.52 pixels, equivalent to 20 m CE90 geolocation accuracy. The resulting geometric consistency improves plume localization and enables more reliable aggregation of repeat detections for identifying persistent methane emitters.

b: The full exploitation of next-generation spaceborne imaging spectrometers requires comprehensive cross-sensor consistency studies spanning different spectral regions and data processing levels. This work presents a two-step comparative analysis of the PRISMA (ASI) and EnMAP (DLR) hyperspectral missions, linking foundational physical measurements in the Visible and Near-Infrared (VNIR) spectrum with high-level environmental products derived in the Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) region. By investigating both a fundamental radiometric variable (Top-of-Atmosphere reflectance) and an advanced derived parameter (methane plume enhancement), this study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of cross-mission interoperability and sensor interchangeability.

The first part of the study focuses on the evaluation of the consistency of TOA reflectance data across the VNIR spectrum. Eleven co-located PRISMA and EnMAP image pairs were analyzed over diverse land cover classes in the Euro-Mediterranean region. The results confirm a strong radiometric correspondence, with the Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM) consistently below 0.1 rad. However, the spectral breakdown reveals varying sensor consistency depending on the wavelength: while the nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) spectral range (420–500 nm) exhibits high alignment (SAM = 0.048, STD = 0.045), the vegetation-sensitive window (750–940 nm) shows larger discrepancies (SAM = 0.097, STD = 0.067), identifying specific bands where cross-sensor data interchange requires careful tuning [1].

The second part shifts the focus to the SWIR region to assess the performance of both PRISMA and EnMAP on an environmental application: the detection and quantification of localized methane emissions. Using the MAG1C retrieval algorithm, the capability of these hyperspectral sensors to resolve methane plumes was evaluated through a multi-sensor comparison. Both satellites successfully reproduced the spatial dynamics and dilution trends along the plume centerlines, demonstrating a high consistency in tracking gas enhancements. Furthermore, the combined use of PRISMA and EnMAP data, cross-examined with high-resolution GHGSat observations for flux estimation (achieving a strong correlation with a Pearson coefficient of 0.95), allowed for the effective reconstruction of a plume's temporal evolution over a two-hour interval [2].

This study demonstrates that despite local discrepancies in specific spectral windows, both sensors offer a highly consistent representation of Earth surface properties and atmospheric dynamics. These findings provide valuable insights for the integration of current hyperspectral datasets, looking forward to the operational capabilities of the upcoming Copernicus CHIME mission.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Anudeep Bildfell<sup>1</sup>, Chad Bryant<sup>1</sup>
b: Wyvern provides high-quality visible and near-infrared (VNIR) hyperspectral imagery as a standard Top-of-Atmosphere radiance (L1B) product and more recently, introduced a surface reflectance (L2A) product. Through removal of atmospheric effects such as aerosols and water vapour, surface reflectance provides a more robust measure of on-ground spectra suitable for use in time-series analysis, machine learning applications, and chemical composition analysis. The MVP release L2A product demonstrated interoperability within the Dragonette constellation and with Sentinel-2 across many terrain types, however residual patterns of discrepancy were found over low reflectance targets such as water and dark forest.

In this presentation we describe ongoing studies to improve the accuracy of the surface reflectance product in three areas. First, we incorporate more calibration targets that help to constrain the regression fit to derive calibration coefficients. The addition of pseudo-invariant sites, deep water targets in Sentinel-2, with more RadCalNet crossovers reduces scatter at low NIR radiance including the oxygen absorption bands. Second, we revisit critical aspects of the atmospheric correction: in anticipation of the upcoming end of MODIS data availability, we transition atmospheric inputs of columnar water vapour and aerosol optical depth to Sentinel-3 and VIIRS, and assess the impact on L2A accuracy over validation sites. We also evaluate the suitability of the Py6S radiative transfer model for Dragonette data in accounting for narrowband terrestrial O₂ and H₂O absorption features. Third, we describe our cross-calibration approach within the Dragonette fleet, leveraging the higher acquisition rate of Dragonette 4 to increase the number of near-simultaneous overpasses available for inter-satellite adjustment. The expanded set of near-simultaneous observations improved spectral consistency across the constellation, yielding a stable, self-consistent Wyvern L2A product for multi-temporal applications.

b: Accurate validation of satellite-derived reflectance products requires a robust assessment of the spatial representativeness of in situ measurements within the satellite observation footprint. For the Fluorescence Explorer (FLEX) mission, with a spatial resolution of approximately 300 m, differences between the scale of ground observations and satellite pixels may introduce significant uncertainties in validation activities, particularly over heterogeneous surfaces.

In this study, we investigate spatial variability and the associated validation uncertainty at a range of established validation sites. Spatial homogeneity indices and spatial representativeness indices are used to quantify the degree to which in situ measurements characterize the surrounding FLEX pixel. The analysis is performed using Sentinel-2 observations, whose higher spatial resolution enables detailed characterization of sub-pixel variability within the FLEX observation footprint.

The methodology is applied to selected sites from the LANDHYPERNET network and FLOX sites established within the INSIF network and within the FRM4FLUO project, covering a range of vegetation types and landscape conditions. By analysing the spatial variability of surface reflectance within a 300 m region of interest, we assess the expected uncertainty arising from scale mismatches between ground-based and satellite observations. The resulting spatial representativeness metrics provide an objective basis for evaluating site suitability for FLEX validation and for quantifying the contribution of spatial heterogeneity to the overall validation uncertainty budget.

Beyond FLEX, the proposed methodology is sensor-independent and can be applied to the validation of higher-resolution satellite missions, provided that observations with sufficiently fine spatial resolution are available to characterize variability within the target pixel or region of interest. Such observations may be obtained from higher-resolution satellite missions, airborne campaigns, or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platforms. The approach therefore provides a general framework for assessing spatial representativeness in Earth observation validation activities across a wide range of spatial scales.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Richard Dobisek<sup>1</sup>
b: The ongoing transition within the Earth Observation (EO) domain from monolithic institutional pipelines to decentralized New Space constellations has significantly increased digital supply chain complexity. While cloud-native infrastructure and edge-computing democratize spatial EO Data, they concurrently expand veracity risks within the EO Data processing chain, also including automated Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning models utilized for object detection and classification. In high-stakes decision-making environments, ensuring data veracity by comprising data integrity, authenticity and traceability has emerged as an operational imperative. In some industries, e.g. dual-use including defence use cases, data veracity is even more critical because unverified or manipulated EO imagery significantly impacts decision-making across strategic, operational, and tactical command tiers. Empirical stakeholder evidence indicates that data integrity is exposed across multiple areas, including both targeted malicious attacks and non-malicious systemic faults. Data integrity can be compromised at several stages along the data supply chain. At the data level, veracity risks include deepfakes, visual content alterations, incorrect location metadata, and tampered timestamps. Within the processing pipelines, also caused unintentionally, the veracity risks include software bugs, version mismatches, and calibration errors, which can degrade data reliability even without a cyberattack. Lastly, malicious actors can intercept data during transmission or tamper directly with processing algorithms and AI models and compromise the EO Data without detection.

To address these risks, an end-to-end data veracity solution is being designed within the VEODDA (Veracity of Earth Observation Data for Defence Applications) project, under the European Defence Agency (EDA) contract and carried out by an international European consortium of seven entities across Slovakia, France, Bulgaria, and Italy. As a result, the VEODDA Solution aims to provide data integrity, immutability and traceability of the EO Data. The technical framework generates lightweight, deterministic cryptographic fingerprints across the entire data lifecycle—starting from the initial sensor perception and processing onboard of the satellites, to the ground segment processing and eventually to end user visualization up to the derived product. These digital fingerprints are anchored onto a decentralized Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) network, establishing an immutable, tamper-evident audit trail that guarantees complete chain-of-custody tracking without requiring an EO Data transmission or exposing proprietary processing logic. The solution architecture establishes a combination of multiple verification mechanisms: handover checks that validate data integrity during network transfers, and processing checks that verify the integrity of the applied algorithms executed during data processing. Integrated directly into user visualization dashboards, the system applies cascading trust logic that translates complex ledger records into intuitive verification badges, enabling end users to inspect full historical provenance trees or generate attested verification reports.

By establishing an immutable, software-driven chain of trust across multi-source Earth Observation pipelines, the VEODDA solution will ensure that imagery, AI model inputs, and derived analytics remain authentic and fully traceable without exposing the EO Data. Ultimately, this solution architecture serves as a foundational baseline for space agencies, commercial operators, and defence stakeholders seeking to establish vendor-agnostic Earth Observation data veracity for confident decision-making.

b: A new orbital regime is being populated without a calibration doctrine. Air-breathing and high-efficiency electric propulsion programmes — ESA's RAM-EP activity, the University of Manchester-led DISCOVERER programme, and commercial developments including drag-compensated very low Earth orbit platforms from several operators — are enabling sustained operation between roughly 180 and 400 km. Optical, infrared, and radar payloads are being proposed for this band, including deployable-antenna L-band concepts recently presented in the community. Yet the calibration and validation practices the Earth Observation community applies to conventional 500–800 km missions were developed under assumptions that do not hold below 400 km, and no framework currently exists for the regime. This contribution presents a systematic assessment of how the calibration problem changes with altitude, based on published atmospheric, ionospheric and materials models rather than flight data, and proposes a candidate framework for community refinement. The headline result is that very low altitude does not degrade all terms uniformly. For low-frequency synthetic aperture radar it materially improves one of the dominant ones. The F2 ionospheric peak typically lies between 250 and 400 km, and a substantial fraction of total electron content lies above it. A sensor operating below the peak therefore traverses only a portion of the electron column seen by a conventional platform. Because Faraday rotation and dispersive phase error both scale inversely with the square of frequency, this is a first-order effect at L-band and below — which is precisely why missions such as NISAR carry split-spectrum ionospheric correction. We further identify a measurement opportunity rather than merely an advantage: a receiver operating below the peak and co-observing the same scene as a conventional-altitude mission offers an independent, geometrically distinct constraint on the ionospheric contribution, derived from differential path rather than from a model or from split-spectrum inversion. Whether that differential signal is separable from geometric, Doppler and system terms at achievable signal-to-noise is posed here as an open question for the community. Five terms nonetheless get harder, and each has a direct calibration consequence. Altitude ceases to be a mission constant: atmospheric density at these altitudes varies by approximately an order of magnitude across the solar cycle, so a drag-compensated platform operates within a control band rather than a frozen orbit, and ground sample distance, incidence angle and swath become per-acquisition variables rather than mission parameters. Aerodynamic disturbance torques scale with density, so platform jitter and the resulting modulation transfer function degradation vary with solar activity, requiring continuous monitoring rather than single characterisation at commissioning. Atomic oxygen fluence is orders of magnitude higher than at conventional altitudes, producing progressive transmittance and emissivity drift in optical windows, coatings and radio-frequency radomes for which heritage degradation models do not transfer. Aerothermal loading on

ram-facing surfaces couples into focal plane thermal stability and therefore radiometric drift. And precise orbit determination is materially harder under high, variable drag, directly degrading geolocation accuracy. Taken together these imply a calibration framework qualitatively different from current practice: per-acquisition rather than per-mission geometric models; continuous rather than episodic modulation transfer function monitoring; substantially higher-cadence radiometric reference observation, supported by onboard witness coupons and dosimetry to separate sensor degradation from environmental degradation; and inter-satellite ranging as a metrology layer supporting orbit determination. Each of these increases the demand on reference infrastructure, which the author addresses in a companion contribution on transportable cross-modal fiducial reference targets. This is a methodology assessment, not a results paper; no flight data are presented. We offer the framework to CEOS WGCV and the EDAP+ community as a starting point for a regime that will shortly require one.

b: At Kuva Space we are building a hyperspectral remote sensing infrastructure to provide high frequency insights at a global scale. By combining spatially and temporally distributed observations from a satellite constellation with advanced data processing and analytics, hyperspectral measurements can be transformed into information on the composition, condition and evolution of observed targets.

The task of combining observations of multiple satellites is non-trival, because the signal measured by remote sensing instruments contains contributions from an ever-changing atmosphere and depends on the viewing and illumination geometry.

Over the last decades, many atmospheric compensation methods have been developed, tailored for specific platforms and applications [1]. Since hyperspectral imagery is highly sensitive to diverse scene contents, researchers typically select tailored atmospheric compensation methods to account for variations in scene brightness, material composition, topography, and adjacency effects that generalized models fail to accurately resolve. At Kuva Space, we distinguish between water and land scenes. Both correction methods adopt slightly different radiative transfer-based models (RTMs), which use the physical knowledge of light propagation to remove the deleterious effect of the atmosphere. Over water, we use an established atmospheric correction method, ACOLITE, [2]), whereas for land scenes, we use an inversion strategy based on RTMs to estimate surface properties, which is the focus of this work.
TRACTOR (Transmission and Reflectance Adjustment by Computing Transfer of Ob-

served Radiometry) is a method based on ATCOR [3] that simplifies the atmosphere-surface interaction (ignoring BRDF and adjacency effects) while maintaining compliance with bottom-of-atmosphere product specifications. It uses the arithmetic inversion of the remote sensing equation based on a simulator with a Libradtran-generated lookup table [4]. Auxiliary atmospheric state information is retrieved from an environmental prediction model (CAMS, [5]), whereas geometric information is obtained from orbital and attitude metadata, enhanced by a digital elevation model. This work provides an overview of the current implementation of the atmospheric correction routine over land, and uses different datasets to provide a benchmark of the method. We use PRISMA imagery as a reference, and compare the performance of TRACTOR against their nominal atmospheric correction method. Furthermore, a glimpse of the performance of TRACTOR-corrected Hyperfield-1 scenes over RadCalNet sites is provided.

b: Agentic AI is redefining the Earth Observation ground segment. Autonomous agents now plan, chain tools, and even create new processing steps on the fly, promising faster, more adaptive RAW-to-L2/L3 pipelines with minimal human intervention. But this shift comes with a hidden cost: as processing paths become dynamic and unpredictable, the very notion of a fixed, auditable pipeline, on which today's integrity and provenance mechanisms largely rely, starts to break down. When an agent decides, in real time, which tool to call or which correction to apply, who can prove what happened to the data, and why?

This presentation addresses the emerging veracity gap opened by agentic AI in EO data chains. We show how multi-agent orchestration multiplies the points at which data can be altered, misattributed, or silently corrected, while making traditional step-by-step verification increasingly impractical. We argue that trust in agentic pipelines cannot be an afterthought, it must be embedded as a first-class capability of the agentic architecture itself.

We then review candidate countermeasures for restoring verifiability in dynamic, self-correcting agent workflows, and illustrate a concrete path forward: a traceability layer embedded directly into the multi-agent pipeline as a dedicated agent, delivering an end-to-end, verifiable proof of data lineage regardless of the actual path taken by the agents.

Looking ahead, we outline a vision for extending the EO Veracity framework to the agentic era: a methodology for building EO pipelines that are not only autonomous, but demonstrably trustworthy, so that speed and adaptability never come at the expense of confidence in the final product.

b: The Optical Mission Performance Cluster (OPT-MPC) is responsible for assessing the maturity and the data quality of thermal/multispectral/hyperspectral Copernicus Contributing Missions (CCMs). CCMs are grouped into three categories: Category 1 includes emerging European EO data providers, Category 2 covers established European data providers, and Category 3 comprises EU or non-EU suppliers providing non-European satellite data. The OPT-MPC activities have been adapted to each category, with the overall objective of ensuring that the data delivered to the Copernicus Services are fit for purpose and meet the expected quality.

For Category 1 CCMs, the assessment follows the Earthnet Data Assessment Pilot (EDAP) framework – an ESA/NASA framework for assessing the suitability of Earth Observation (EO) missions - and addresses both the completeness of the documentation (the user guide, cal/val plan, and ATBD) and the quality of the data products through independent data validation. The OPT-MPC also supports Cat.1 CCMs in their Cal/Val activities by providing guidance with standards and good practices. Recently, the OPT-MPC introduced a Data Quality Statement (DQS) to regularly share a summary of the independent validation results with CCMs and for communication to the relevant Copernicus Services. The assessment is quarterly updated. The first operational data samples were also successfully delivered to the Copernicus Services. For Category 2 & 3 CCMs, the activities performed focus on the monitoring of sensor performance and on data quality assessment dedicated to evaluating data suitability for applications such as the “VHR Coverage of Europe" (e.g., VHR_IMAGE_2024) and VHR DG-AGRI Coverage activities.

This presentation will focus on the OPT-MPC framework for CCMs and its recent adaptations. An overview of the reference standards, lessons learned, and key L1 data quality metrics will be provided, along with a presentation of the ongoing activities. Finally, for Cat.1 CCMs, expectations for their respective phases of the program in terms of data delivery and quality will be outlined.

b: The increasing demand for sovereign, responsive and persistent Earth Observation capabilities is driving the development of compact Very-High-Resolution (VHR) optical payloads towards higher spatial resolution, improved image quality, shorter latency and operation over an extended range of illumination conditions. Within this context, cosine is developing the Valk™ family of optical instruments as part of a technology roadmap initiated within the Dutch PAMI programme.

The first generation of Valk establishes a compact VHR visible imaging capability designed for integration on microsatellite-class platforms. The development addresses the complete imaging chain, from optical design and focal-plane performance to thermo-mechanical stability, line-of-sight knowledge, on-board processing and geometric and radiometric calibration. Particular attention is given to the relationship between payload-level performance and the resulting end-to-end image quality, including MTF, SNR, geolocation accuracy and stability.

The roadmap subsequently extends the architecture in two complementary directions. A next-generation Valk instrument increases aperture and focal length to progress towards sub-metre and ultimately Ultra-High-Resolution imaging while retaining compatibility with relatively compact spacecraft. In parallel, Valk™ Nox extends the concept towards low-luminance and night-time imaging in the infrared. Together, these developments establish a path from individual VHR instruments towards complementary day, twilight and night observation capabilities.

The paper will present the Valk technology roadmap and discuss the principal performance challenges associated with scaling compact optical instruments towards increasingly demanding spatial resolution.

Finally, the contribution will discuss how common calibration approaches and instrument architectures can support the evolution from individual demonstrators towards coordinated multi-satellite VHR systems, providing consistent and traceable data products across successive generations of sensors.

b: Absolute Radiometric Calibration is necessary for deriving accurate physical measurements from remote sensing systems. Satellites lacking on-board calibration devices must rely on instrumented calibration sites (RadCalNet or similar calibration networks) or natural targets, such as Pseudo-Invariant Calibration Sites (PICS) or the Moon. Stars have been proposed as absolute radiometric references due to their immunity to atmospheric disturbances, year-round availability, and spectral/magnitude properties that accommodate dynamic ranges for a wide set of sensors.

Although star-based radiometric calibration methods have been discussed for over two decades [1] and implemented for the Pleiades HR satellites [2] [3], a generic uncertainty estimation framework remains absent from the literature. This study provides a decomposition of uncertainty contributors to the star-based absolute radiometric calibration process. Radiometric model parameters uncertainties are accounted for analytically using a sensor-independent method, while measurement errors are evaluated via simulations to determine sensitivity to global parameters, including Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Point Spread Function (PSF) characteristics.

The proposed framework is demonstrated using star measurements from the Pleiades NEO Very-High-Resolution constellation. Based on the Gaia DR3 catalogue, uncertainty in the star irradiance spectrum is identified as a primary contributor to the total uncertainty budget. Furthermore, we show that measurement-induced uncertainty can be mitigated through rigorous star selection and the accumulation of multiple measurements.

This study proposes an uncertainty budget for star-based absolute radiometric calibration using a combination of analytical modelling and simulations. Numerical results provide useful insights for the selection of suitable star targets and image acquisition strategies.

b: Super KARIOS is a scripted application that wraps the KARIOS tool into an automated process that takes a user-selected list of ground control points and tiles of qualified imagery or LIDAR data, runs a per-tile KARIOS accuracy assessment, and then accumulates the results into a KARIOS-like statistical analysis across the family of selected tiles. With the advent of public-facing, nationally federated LIDAR data sets, it is possible to automate the evaluation of drone, airborne, and satellite imagery against both LIDAR imagery and LIDAR-derived surface models.

Critical to this process is the Independent Verification and Validation (IV&V) of the reference surface and imagery data. In the United States, the USGS’s 3DEP program provides LIDAR point clouds for calibration and ground control points for independent verification and validation[1,2]. Shean [3] has automated the integration of collection metadata and the IV&V of selected tiles using the USGS, NGS, and FAA ground control databases. Similar analyses are being automated within the context of the ESA’s GCPIX [4] initiative by using GCP Viewer data [5] (Grosseto test site in Italy and the La Crau test site in France).

Preliminary results at the Casa Grande Photogrammetric Test Range, located near Casa Grande, AZ, demonstrate the IV&V process and the application of Super KARIOS to the evaluation of public-facing basemaps including USDA’s NAIP, Bing, Google, and ESRI using 115 1-square-kilometer sites, each of which contain a 60-foot concrete photogrammetric cross target.

With regards to metric calibration of sensors, we find that the accuracy of the Bing, Google, and ESRI data are not sufficient for VHR image calibration with an average accuracy of ~ 2.2-2.5 m CE90 relative to the 3DEP Lidar database. In contrast, the consistency of the USDA NAIP imagery products may support VHR imagery calibration with an average accuracy of < 0.6-1.06 m CE90 [6-8] using traditional survey ground control which we independently validated relative to the USGS 3DEP LIDAR with an accuracy of 0.8 m CE90. Following completion of independent validation and software testing, Super KARIOS will be released within the existing open-source KARIOS framework. The preliminary results indicate that quality-controlled national LIDAR and recent NAIP imagery can provide substantially stronger reference data for automated VHR image assessment than the tested commercial basemaps. A KARIOS cloud solution is a logical service extension for consideration in 2027.

b: Stable, traceable ground references are required to distinguish true surface displacement from motion of the reference structure and from errors introduced by the observing and processing systems. This distinction is especially important for very-high-resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR) calibration and validation, where a precisely surveyed reflector can still be unsuitable if its foundation, structure, or electromagnetic phase center moves seasonally. We synthesize International GNSS Service (IGS) operational guidance, published GNSS monument-performance evidence, and experience from integrated geodetic reference stations to propose testable acceptance criteria for colocated continuous GNSS (cGNSS), SAR, and levelling infrastructure.

The IGS guidelines require stable long-term operation, suitable foundations, repeatable antenna mounting, complete metadata, and marker-to-antenna-reference-point eccentricities surveyed to 1 mm or better [1]. They do not prescribe quantitative limits for wind deflection, thermal motion, or unexplained drift. Site geology should be characterized by a qualified geoscientist, preferably a licensed professional geologist, to ensure that monument design is appropriate for the local geologic conditions and the station’s intended measurement objectives. We therefore identify the following as proposed engineering criteria rather than existing IGS requirements: anchorage below active soil and frost effects; predicted GNSS and SAR reference-point movement of 1 mm or less under environmental loading, with 0.5 mm preferred under normal wind; GNSS antenna remounting repeatability of 0.5 mm or better; reflector installation centering below 1 mm and orientation within 1 degree; local three-dimensional ties among the permanent monument marker, GNSS antenna geodetic reference point, SAR phase center, and levelling marks measured to 1 mm or better with covariance and reference epoch; initial SAR signal-to-clutter ratio of at least 20 dB, with 25–30 dB preferred; and monitoring over at least one complete seasonal cycle before acceptance as a stable reference.

Published GNSS coordinate scatter provides a system-level performance benchmark, not a direct measurement of monument motion. Herring et al. [2] found that deep-drilled braced monuments (DDBMs), consisting of five legs extending approximately 10 m into underlying rock or sediment, with the upper 4 m of each leg isolated from near-surface soil movement, had the lowest median residual scatter and horizontal random-walk noise among the monument classes examined. Their reported median weighted root-mean-square (WRMS) values were 0.9 mm north, 1.0 mm east, and 4.9 mm up; the corresponding 95th-percentile values were approximately 2.2, 2.4, and 7.0 mm. These statistics also include atmospheric, multipath, environmental, geophysical, reference-frame, and processing effects.

As a regional demonstration, we analyzed 19 TU Delft-hosted Integrated Geodetic Reference Station time series from 2019–2025. The median horizontal radial and vertical WRMS residuals were 0.788 and 1.026 mm, respectively. For station ENGE over the common 16 January 2019–27 September 2025 interval, the TU Delft NAM state-space-representation solution produced radial and vertical WRMS values of 0.597 and 0.691 mm. The independent Nevada Geodetic Laboratory IGS20 precise-point-positioning solution produced 1.711 and 5.536 mm, respectively—approximately 2.9 and 8.0 times larger. The difference demonstrates the influence of processing strategy and reference-frame realization; it does not imply different physical monument behavior.

We conclude that future cGNSS–SAR requirements should separate structural stability, measurement-system repeatability, absolute geolocation accuracy, and processing-dependent coordinate scatter. Integrated stations such as those in the Netherlands provide a practical architecture for testing these quantities through cGNSS time series, SAR amplitude and phase histories, levelling, environmental instrumentation, and repeated terrestrial ties. A global requirements effort should apply this traceable framework across diverse monument types, climates, geology, and processing strategies before adopting universal numerical thresholds.
[1] International GNSS Service (2026) Guidelines for Continuously Operating Reference Stations in the IGS, version 1.1. IGS guidelines.

[2] Herring, T.A. et al. (2016) ‘Plate Boundary Observatory and related networks: GPS data analysis methods and geodetic products’, Reviews of Geophysics, 54(4), pp. 759– 808. https://doi.org/10.1002/2016RG000529.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Wolfgang Lueck<sup>1</sup>
b: Sentinel-2's wide-swath, high-revisit optical archive is a valuable source for maritime domain awareness, but the quality of the delivered CEOS Analysis-Ready Data (ARD) has a direct, measurable effect on two very different downstream tasks: finding a vessel, and characterising its motion. We report on both, using a four-band Red, NIR, SWIR1.6, SWIR2.2 stack processed through EOIntelligence's IRMI™ platform.

For detection, well-calibrated, consistently aligned bands allowed us to rescale the 16-bit stack to 8-bit for GPU-based YOLO inference using a single, stable set of per-band clip ranges applied across a whole campaign, rather than a per-scene adjustment. This preserved the maximum usable dynamic range for dark-hulled vessels against a water background whose reflectance collapses in the near-infrared and shortwave-infrared, and improved the consistency of our detector relative to a naive global stretch. For movement intelligence, we exploit a property of Sentinel-2's own acquisition geometry: its bands are captured by physically offset detector arrays at slightly different instants within a single pass, so a moving vessel's true inter-band offset differs measurably from the offset a stationary scene would produce. Good band-to-band alignment in the delivered product is what makes this offset measurable by sub-pixel phase correlation in the first place, and it is what let us recover a vessel's speed and heading from a single pass.

The same result also exposes a limitation. The precision with which we can characterise motion is bounded, in part, by the residual band misalignment already present in the ARD product before our own geometric model and matching are applied. A tighter initial co-registration between bands would translate directly into a tighter velocity and heading estimate downstream, without any change to our own algorithms. We use this as a concrete case for the conference: ARD calibration and alignment quality are not solely a cartographic or radiometric concern, but a first-order input to the achievable accuracy of the analytic products built on top of them, and we would welcome closer engagement between processing teams and ARD product developers on where that accuracy currently sits.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Keith Beckett<sup>1</sup>
b: The EarthDaily Analytics team is actively building a constellation of highly innovative satellites, capable of covering the earth’s landmass every day with a novel set of spectral channels selected to serve a wide range of applications. To-date, 8 of the 10 satellites are now on orbit and being commissioned. The resulting data will flflow through our EarthPipeline, a completely automated Ground Segment-as-a-Service offffering, capable of processing, calibrating and validating not only the data from EarthDaily Analytics’ constellation but data from multiple partners’ constellations as well.

We know that nearly every application targeted by EarthDaily Analytics, agriculture, forestry, water and many more, will all benefifit greatly from the science-grade imagery and analytics that the EarthPipeline will deliver. With novel spectral channels, ranging from visible through to thermal, combined with the objective to deliver high-value imagery and analytics, comes several calibration and validation challenges.

This presentation will provide an update on our progress with the EarthDaily constellation, and will delve into our rigorous pre- and post-launch cal/val processes, and discuss how we will ultimately address these various challenges in order to achieve the radiometric, geometric and retrieval accuracy requirements necessary to achieve the science-grade data products.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Isla Duporge<sup>1</sup>
b: Over the past decade, commercial very high-resolution (VHR) optical satellites have become a working survey tool for large animals. Deep learning models can be used in conjunction with VHR satellite images to fifind elephants in mixed savanna and woodland, count wildebeest across the Serengeti, and pick out whales at the sea surface. What has not yet been achieved is making the resulting numbers trustworthy enough to feed directly into management decisions. This gap is a calibration and validation problem, and it is one the earth-observation satellite community is better equipped to solve than the ecologists currently carrying it.

In this talk I will use terrestrial and marine examples from my own research to show where validation fails. An animal covers just one to four pixels at 31 cm resolution, so whether it is seen at all depends on offff-nadir angle, radiometric quality, atmospheric correction, and how the image was preprocessed. Reference data are the harder problem. Coincident ground counts almost never exist; aerial surveys carry their own detection and availability biases; and because animals move, even a small gap between the image and the reference survey introduces error. At sea, add the fraction of animals visible at the surface, plus sea state and glint.

My aim is to put some priorities on the table: open reference datasets spanning species and habitats, intercalibration protocols so counts can be compared across sensors, and uncertainty carried all the way through to the population estimate rather than stopping at precision and recall.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.f: <sup>1</sup>Labsphere, Inc., North Sutton, United States, <sup>2</sup>CalVal Research, La Mirada, United States
b: Absolute radiometric interoperability among modern Earth-observing sensor constellations requires calibration methods that establish physically equivalent measurements among independent imaging systems. While conventional vicarious calibration emphasizes scene radiance as the reference quantity, imaging detectors respond fundamentally to optical irradiance at the sensor entrance aperture, suggesting that irradiance provides a more direct basis for detector characterization and absolute calibration. This paper presents an irradiance-based calibration framework founded on SI-traceable point-source measurements generated using the SPecular Array Radiometric Calibration (SPARC) methodology and its commercial implementation, FLARE. Calibrated artificial solar point sources with known at-sensor irradiance directly characterize detector response while reducing uncertainties associated with extended diffuse calibration targets. Building on this principle, the paper introduces Point Target Responsive Radiometry, which characterizes detector response as a function of radiometric level, focal-plane position, temporal stability, and sensor geometry using controlled SI-traceable point-source stimuli. These measurements establish a Common Radiometric State through which independent sensors are referenced to a common irradiance standard, enabling quantitative comparison of detector performance independent of instrument architecture. The framework demonstrates how a single SI-traceable point-source measurement supports absolute calibration, constellation harmonization, temporal gain monitoring, sensor characterization, and geometric image registration. Rather than replacing conventional radiance-based image products, the proposed methodology strengthens their absolute accuracy and long-term consistency by providing a unified SI-traceable measurement architecture for detector calibration, constellation harmonization, and sensor interoperability.

b: ACOLITE (github.com/acolite/acolite) is a free and open source (GPL-3) tool for the processing of optical and thermal satellite imagery. It includes several algorithms for the atmospheric correction of metre, decametre, and kilometre scale satellite imagery. The algorithms in ACOLITE were originally designed for inland and coastal water applications, but most of them can also be used for land applications.

In this interactive training session, participants will be introduced to the processing of metre scale optical satellite imagery using ACOLITE. The provided materials will cover basic setting configuration, and a comparison of the Dark Spectrum Fitting (DSF), and Remote sensing Adjacency Correction (RAdCor) atmospheric correction options. The download of this image is integrated within the notebook and online runtime, and no local storage will be required. Basic plotting of results from the NetCDF outputs will be performed within the notebooks, but for those who wish to further explore the output NetCDF products, the use of SNAP (step.esa.int/main/download/snap-download/) is recommended.

b: DIVA (Demonstration of an Integrated approach for the Validation and exploitation of Atmospheric missions, https://www.diva-platform.com/) is a collaborative python jupyter notebook-based platform aiming to collect, handle, and exploit atmospheric data from satellite, ground-based remote sensing instruments, in-situ and modelling products and to build new synergies and validation approaches beyond the operational products.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.f: <sup>1</sup>VITO Remote Sensing, Mol, Belgium, <sup>2</sup>ESA ESTEC, Noordwijk, The Netherlands, <sup>3</sup>ESA ESRIN, Italy
b: IPERLITE is a new Belgian In Orbit Demonstration hyperspectral Earth observation mission led by VITO Remote Sensing, designed to demonstrate compact, high-performance imaging from a small satellite platform. Built on Aerospacelab's VSP-150 platform, the mission carries CSIMBA (Compact Smartspectral Imager for Monitoring Bio-agricultural Areas), an innovative hyperspectral sensor based on thin-film interference filters deposited directly on a CMOS detector. Unlike conventional dispersive spectrometers, CSIMBA relies on a linear variable filter (LVF) architecture, enabling a compact, robust instrument design. It captures up to 154 spectral bands across the 465–900 nm visible and near-infrared (VNIR) range, at 20 m ground sampling distance over an 80 km swath, with digital Time Delay Integration (TDI) enhancing radiometric performance. A key challenge of this push-broom LVF architecture is the temporal offset between spectral bands inherent to the acquisition sequence, which introduces inter-band geometric misregistration requiring dedicated co-registration during processing.

This paper presents the challenges and final in-orbit calibration and validation results from the mission's commissioning phase, covering its geometric, radiometric and spectral performance, and the validation of the operational Level-1C/2A processing chain. In addition to traditional vicarious calibration methods over Pseudo-Invariant Calibration Sites (PICS) and RadCalNet sites, dedicated Moon acquisitions and a 90° yaw manoeuvre were performed to support radiometric calibration and characterization of the instrument's response. The results confirm the maturity of the IPERLITE processing chain and the mission's readiness to deliver calibrated hyperspectral data products for scientific use. Initial cross-comparisons with EnMAP show very promising agreement, and a future comparison with PRISMA is planned to further consolidate the instrument's radiometric and spectral performance assessment. Following the successful completion of commissioning in early July 2026, IPERLITE has now entered its operational phase, and the scientific community is invited to apply for access to its hyperspectral data.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Stein Rune Karlsen<sup>1</sup>, Andrew Gray<sup>2</sup>, Matteo Crespin-Jouan<sup>3</sup>, Kristoffer Aalstad<sup>3</sup>, Norbert Pirk<sup>3</sup>, Lennart Nilsen<sup>4</sup>, Kjell-Arild Høgda<sup>1</sup>, Hans Tømmervik<sup>2</sup>

b: Validation of the forthcoming ESA FLEX Level 2C vegetation products — Leaf Area Index (LAI), Leaf Chlorophyll Content (LCC), and fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (fAPAR) — requires spatially representative, high-resolution reference datasets matched to the 300 m FLEX pixel size. This is particularly demanding in High-Arctic tundra, where vegetation is sparse and heterogeneous at sub-metre scales, driven by variation in active layer depth and the position of the water table. Bryophytes dominate large areas and constitute the main plant biomass across much of the landscape, yet are largely invisible to standard optical retrieval algorithms calibrated for vascular plant canopies.

Our study site is Adventdalen, Svalbard (78.1°N, 15.6°E), where the convergence of polar orbits provides an exceptional observational advantage: Sentinel-2 acquires three images per day within approximately two hours, enabling a temporally dense time series that is unmatched at lower latitudes and well suited to capturing the short, rapidly evolving High-Arctic growing season.

The ground infrastructure in Adventdalen is extensive. Ten cal/val racks distributed across the main tundra types continuously record PAR (Photosynthetically Active Radiation), PRI (Photochemical Reflectance Index), and NDVI alongside standard climate variables. Permanent field sites provide phenological observations and plant productivity measurements. Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is measured both from a fixed FLoX spectrometer rack and from an airborne AirFloX instrument mounted on a UAV, enabling simultaneous point-scale and spatially distributed SIF retrievals during FLEX overpass windows.

High-resolution vegetation mapping is central to the validation framework. A regularly scheduled passenger aircraft equipped with a HySpex airborne hyperspectral imager, based at Svalbard Airport adjacent to the study site, acquires imagery during peak growing season. These data are used to derive fine-scale maps of plant functional groups and vegetation types, and to retrieve key biophysical variables including LAI, LCC, PRI, and fAPAR at species and plant community levels — a spatial detail not achievable with any spaceborne sensor currently available.

The SvalFLEX project (ESA PRODEX PEA No. 4000152491) integrates these datasets within a multi-scale validation framework. In-situ field measurements anchor the finest scale; HySpex hyperspectral products provide intermediate spatial detail; and a cloud-free Sentinel-2 time series, upscaled using a super-resolution model trained on the hyperspectral data, provides the temporally dense wall-to-wall coverage needed for aggregation to the 300 m FLEX pixel. We present initial results illustrating the spatial variability of vegetation properties across the study domain, the performance of the multi-scale upscaling chain for High-Arctic tundra, and the implications for FLEX Level 2C validation at latitudes where existing Copernicus land products are either absent or unreliable.

b: Reducing global methane emissions is vital in combating climate change. Satellite-based instruments provide a way to independently monitor methane emissions from various sources at different scales, helping to assess the progress toward emission reduction targets. In this study, we apply several data-driven methods to estimate methane emissions from the Secunda CTL (coal-to-liquids) synthetic fuel plant in South Africa, utilizing satellite observations from the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) aboard the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5P) satellite, and the GHGSat fleet of high-resolution commercial satellites. We find annual mean emissions of about 13-22 t/h based on S5P/TROPOMI observations. These results are consistent with estimates from an automated TROPOMI methane plume detection and quantification method. Estimates based on GHGSat observations from individual sources within the plant sum to about 6 t/h on average. For comparison, Sasol, the operator of the Secunda CTL facility, reported methane emissions of 11.5 t/h for the period July 2023-June 2024, a value that falls between the TROPOMI- and GHGSat-based estimates. Our results highlight the value of satellite observations as a useful audit complementing reported emissions and demonstrate the importance of combining coarse- and fine-resolution data to monitor methane emissions at plant and intra-facility level in complex sources. This research is part of the activities carried out at the Finnish Meteorological Institute for the development of the Emission Observatory platform (https://www.emissionobservatory.org) and within the METSA (METhane emissions from South Africa's Secunda synthetic fuel plant) ESA Third Party Mission project. Most of the results of the project are included in the journal article by Virta et al. (Environ. Sci. Technol. Lett. 2026).

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Pavel Lytvynov<sup>1</sup>, Christian Matar<sup>1</sup>, Smita Panda<sup>1</sup>, Oleg Dubovik<sup>2</sup>, David Fuertes<sup>1</sup>, Silvia Scifoni<sup>3</sup>, Philippe Goryl<sup>4</sup>

b: The characterizations of the atmosphere and underlying surface from remote sensing are closely related problems. One of the grand science challenges in remote sensing and climate studies is the accurate separation of surface and atmosphere contributions to the satellite signal. For accurate characterization of both aerosol and surface, the new approach based on the synergy of the GROund based and SATellite measurements (GROSAT) was developed (eo4society.esa.int/projects/grosat/). In such GROSAT approach both ground-based (AERONET) and satellite measurements are merged together and then the synergetic aerosol and surface retrieval is performed on the combined measurements.

The main information about aerosol in the GROSAT synergy comes from AERONET direct sun and diffuse sky-radiance measurements, whereas the information about surface reflection properties originates from satellite observations. The simultaneous retrieval of aerosol and surface properties in GROSAT approach is performed with GRASP (Generalized Retrieval of Aerosol and Surface Properties) algorithm.

Due to rich information content about aerosol in the ground-based measurements like AERONET, GROSAT synergetic approach allows for accurate separation of aerosol and surface signals. It is easy adjustable to different space-borne measurements with different spectral and spatial resolution. In this sense, GROSAT approach allows robust generation of the surface reference dataset in worldwide locations for any specified spectral bands, spectral and spatial resolution.

The accurate surface product from the synergetic GRASP ground-based (AERONET) + satellite retrieval approach can be obtained under the condition that the instruments are well calibrated or the information about instrument calibration is known. If this is not the case, the synergetic approach can be applied to different satellites, one of which is well-calibrated. In this way, analyzing biases in the obtained surface products and residuals of measurement fits, the synergetic approach can be used for cross-calibration of the instruments. In this talk we present GROSAT generated surface reference datasets and discuss possibility of using GROSAT approach for satellite instruments cross-calibration.
