https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.f: <sup>1</sup>European Space Agency / ESTEC, Noordwijk, Netherlands, <sup>2</sup>European Space Agency / ESRIN, Frascati, Italy
b: The European Space Agency is currently developing a suite of Sentinel expansion missions as well as the next generation follow ups to replace Sentinels-1, -2, and -3. While defining the needs and requirements for these missions, we have received significant user feedback indicating that night observations should be considered as an operational component.

As such, we performed night-time acquisitions with Sentinel-2A and Sentinel-3A to assess the value of night data for a variety of use cases such as urban lights, shipping monitoring, wildfire and gas flare detection, and volcano monitoring. This presentation will examine the radiometric performance of the S2 and S3 sensor suites during night time observations, highlighting limitations and potential use cases.

Finally, while noting that no commitment is made to any night imaging, the presentation will examine the potential feasibility of scenarios for a limited set of night-time observations in the scope of the upcoming LSTM, Sentinel-2 Next Generation and Sentinel-3 Next Generation missions.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: James O'Connor<sup>1</sup>
b: The emergence of increasingly agile Earth observation platforms, including those likely to form part of programmes such as ERS-EO, creates new opportunities for responsive and targeted imaging. Satellites able to point far from nadir can increase access, revisit opportunities and acquisition flexibility, but they also challenge some of the assumptions that underpin conventional approaches to Analysis Ready Data (ARD), towards CEOS-ARD goal requirements.

In principle ARD is intended to reduce the burden on users by providing data that can be used with minimal additional processing. In doing so, however, it can encourage assumptions of consistency and comparability that become harder to sustain as acquisition geometries become more diverse. Concepts such as a consistent spatial grid or uniform geometric quality are relatively natural for sensors operating within constrained viewing geometries. For highly agile systems, observations of the same location may instead be acquired from substantially different angles, ranges and illumination conditions, with consequences that cannot always be removed through preprocessing alone.

These effects are influenced by a range of parameters that may sit beneath the level at which many users interact with ARD: viewing and illumination geometry, terrain and ancillary data quality, geolocation uncertainty, resampling, atmospheric path length, resolution and observation geometry, among others. As these dependencies become less visible to the user, there is a risk that “analysis ready” is interpreted as meaning that observations are interchangeable when, for some applications, they are not.

This presentation considers the gaps and opportunities that agile platforms introduce for ARD. Addressing these questions will be important if the flexibility offered by the next generation of agile EO systems is to be exploited without hiding the consequences of that flexibility from downstream users.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Francesco Pasanisi<sup>1</sup>, Tom Hendrix<sup>1</sup>, David Rijlaarsdam<sup>1</sup>, Aubrey Dunne<sup>2</sup>
https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.f: <sup>1</sup>Ubotica Technologies, Delft, Netherlands, <sup>2</sup>Ubotica Technologies, Dublin, Ireland
b: Off-nadir image acquisition substantially increases the revisit frequency of agile imaging satellites such as CogniSAT-6, yet its impact on deep learning model performance for ship segmentation remains unstudied. This paper presents an evaluation of off-nadir acquisition (ONA) effects on a CNN-based ship segmentation model, using 38 annotated CogniSAT-6 scenes spanning the full 0°–45° roll angle range, organized into four viewing angle bins. Contrary to findings from building detection studies, no statistically significant relationship was found between viewing angle and model performance (R²=0.030, p=0.302). Spearman correlation analysis revealed that roll angle, sun zenith angle, and median ship size are not significant predictors of performance. Instead, the ship-water contrast ratio emerged as the only significant predictor (r=0.563, p<0.001), indicating that scene-specific spectral characteristics are a stronger determinant of segmentation quality than acquisition geometry. These findings suggest that CogniSAT-6 can operate across its full roll angle range without significant degradation in ship segmentation performance, with scene spectral characteristics being the primary factor to take into account.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Panagiotis Agrafiotis<sup>1</sup>, Stylianos Kossieris<sup>1</sup>, Georgios Tsilimanis<sup>1</sup>, Theodoros Giannakas<sup>1</sup>, Elisavet Parselia<sup>2</sup>, Dimitrios Bliziotis<sup>3</sup>, Georgios Tsimiklis<sup>2</sup>, Angelos Amditis<sup>1</sup>
https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.f: <sup>1</sup>Institute Of Communication And Computer Systems (ICCS), Athens, Greece, <sup>2</sup>CogniSensus, Athens, Greece, <sup>3</sup>Hellenic Space Center, Athens, Greece
b: Robust validation of satellite-derived thermal products requires well-characterized reference sites that combine spatial homogeneity, thermal stability, representativeness, and accessibility. Within the framework of the Greek National Satellite Space Project’s Thermal Space Segment, a reference test site has been established to support the validation of space-based thermal observations. The land site is located in Arcadia, Greece, covering an area of approximately 0.155 km². The site is characterized by a flat landscape and sparse vegetation, providing high spatial homogeneity and stable emissivity characteristics. Moderate diurnal and seasonal thermal variations, together with low annual variability, further support its suitability for thermal satellite validation. The equipment obtained for the validation campaigns is a high-precision CIMEL CE312-N2 radiometer with six spectral bands, Apogee infrared thermometers, soil-moisture sensors for surface characterization, and a weather station. Continuous measurements at Arcadia are provided by an Apogee thermometer installed at approximately 3 m height, three soil-moisture sensors for surface characterization, and a weather station. The combination of high-precision and lower-cost sensors provides an effective balance between measurement accuracy, operational flexibility, and campaign scalability. In addition, the portability of CIMEL CE312 radiometer provides flexibility for deployment at different locations according to the scientific objectives of individual Cal/Val campaigns. The radiometer could therefore be used at sites presenting challenging conditions for thermal retrievals, including heterogeneous surfaces, coastal zones, urban and agricultural areas, and regions with strong thermal gradients.

The Cal/Val framework is complemented by measurements over the sea. An Apogee thermometer has been installed on the Typhoon vessel to acquire sea surface temperature (SST) measurements. The sensor is accompanied by a GNSS receiver, providing the geographic position of each SST observation and enabling georeferenced measurements during vessel operations. By combining continuous ground-based measurements at a stable reference site, mobile marine observations, and portable high-precision radiometer measurements, the proposed Greek Land–Sea TIR Cal/Val framework provides a flexible approach for the validation of thermal satellite products across complementary land and sea environments. It also offers the capability to support targeted measurement campaigns for current and future thermal Earth observation missions.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Idurre Barinagarrementeria Arrese<sup>1</sup>, Gemma Ventura<sup>1</sup>
b: Monitoring the stability of critical civil infrastructure is essential for ensuring safety, supporting maintenance activities, and mitigating risks associated with ground deformation in urban environments. Persistent Scatterer Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (PS-DInSAR) provides an effective framework for measuring millimetric displacements over large areas using radar satellite data. This study evaluates the suitability of the Spanish PAZ X-band SAR mission for infrastructure monitoring through a comparison with the Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band mission over the Hambach region in Germany. The analysis was performed using 50 PAZ acquisitions and 88 Sentinel-1 images acquired between 2021 and 2022.

The PS-DInSAR processing focused on transport-related infrastructure, including airport runways, roads, bridges, and railway corridors. Persistent scatterers were identified and analysed to assess the capability of both satellite missions to detect and monitor ground deformation. Due to its higher spatial resolution, PAZ identified approximately 2.7 million persistent scatterers, significantly exceeding the approximately 300,000 points detected by Sentinel-1.

Results showed a strong agreement between deformation estimates derived from both datasets, confirming the reliability of PAZ measurements. Additionally, the higher density of persistent scatterers provided by PAZ enabled a more detailed characterization of infrastructure stability, particularly over flat surfaces where deformation monitoring is often challenging.

The study demonstrates the added value of high-resolution X-band SAR data for urban infrastructure monitoring and highlights the potential of PAZ to complement established Sentinel-1 deformation monitoring services.

b: ICEYE operates the largest commercial SAR satellite fleet, which continues to grow rapidly. To keep pace with the rate at which new satellites are commissioned, major parts of the commissioning process have been automated. Azimuth ambiguities and large antenna azimuth mispointing are two of the major contributors to degraded image quality in spaceborne SAR systems, and both can be characterised by exploiting the skewed signature in the two-dimensional spectrum. Automating the assessment of azimuth ambiguity levels requires replacing manual inspection of the imagery with an objective numerical metric. This presentation describes a fully automatic technique that separates ambiguous from unambiguous energy directly in the SAR data, and shows how the same measurement supports both azimuth ambiguity assessment and the estimation of large antenna pointing errors.

Azimuth ambiguities, folded in from outside the processed Doppler bandwidth, retain a coupling between range and azimuth frequencies that the nominal matched filter does not compensate for, and therefore appear as skewed signatures with respect to the unambiguous data. The nominal processing focuses the true scene and leaves the ambiguous energy smeared, so the two components can be distinguished by how well focused they are.

The method applies a phase scan to exploit this. The two-dimensional spectrum of the data is multiplied by a linear phase coupling the range and azimuth frequencies, which deskews the ambiguous contribution in a keystone-like manner but, unlike conventional keystone formatting, requires no resampling and therefore introduces no interpolation loss. The coefficient governing this phase is estimated by iterating over candidate values and selecting the one that maximises the refocused ambiguous peak. After deskewing the spectrum with the optimal coefficient, an inverse DFT returns the data to the image domain, where the ambiguous energy is now localised while the previously focused scene energy is smeared. Because focusing of the two components is mutually exclusive, the localised peak can be integrated and compared to the unambiguous energy measured in the nominally focused image, yielding absolute and relative ambiguity figures without any assumption about scene content.
Application to Ambiguity Assessment and Pointing Error Estimation

Applied to ambiguity assessment, the extracted ratio provides a direct, quantitative measure of the ambiguity level of an acquisition, usable both as an ambiguity metric and as a pass/fail criterion against a defined threshold. A non-ideal azimuth antenna pattern with elevated sidelobes would appear here as increased ambiguous energy.

The same method can be applied, with no change to the underlying processing, to antenna pointing verification. In this case the roles are reversed: it is the mainlobe return, not the ambiguity, that appears skewed, and the same phase scan recovers it. When large off-pointing occurs, the image is focused to the intended imaging area illuminated by a sidelobe. The mainlobe return therefore arrives at a Doppler centroid far from the processed one, leaving residual range cell migration that the nominal range cell migration correction does not remove. This causes a skew in the mainlobe’s two-dimensional spectrum that can be exploited to estimate the amount of off-pointing based on the angle of the skew and known satellite geometry.

By discriminating ambiguous from unambiguous energy through refocusing rather than through geometric separation, the technique delivers an interpolation-free, scene-independent and fully automatic measurement. Its dual use for ambiguity assessment and pointing error estimation makes it well suited to a systematic azimuth antenna pattern and pointing assessment chain during commissioning and routine calibration.

b: The Country Awareness Mission in Land Analysis (CAMILA) is the Polish National Earth Observation program developed through technical assistance agreement between the Polish Ministry of Economic Development and Technology (MRIT) and the European Space Agency (ESA).

Currently undergoing Preliminary Design Review (PDR), the mission is based on a hybrid constellation combining very-high-resolution optical, low-resolution optical, and X-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites.
The constellation is intended to provide a broad range of civil applications through the delivery of complementary optical and SAR products.

The coexistence of optical and SAR sensors within a single constellation introduces challenges in calibration, validation, product verification, and long-term data quality assurance. Beyond the characterization of individual instruments, the mission must ensure traceability, consistency, and user confidence across heterogeneous products, and processing chains. This paper presents the calibration, validation, and product quality framework currently being developed for CAMILA as part of the mission design activities. The proposed concept combines on-ground characterization, commissioning calibration activities, routine validation, and operational recalibration processes into a unified lifecycle supporting both mission operations and long-term product quality monitoring.

The CAMILA Payload Data Ground Segment (PDGS) hosts two dedicated processing chains, and Calibration and Validation (Cal/Val) environment for both optical and SAR data. This architecture maintains payload-specific calibration baselines, quality monitoring activities, and performance assessment processes while ensuring traceability throughout product generation. A key objective is to establish a direct link between calibration activities and end-product quality. Calibration and validation results are propagated through the processing chains and assessed against mission-level performance indicators, enabling end-to-end verification of data quality from raw acquisitions to operational products. For the optical segment, verification activities focus on image quality, radiometric and geometric performance through metrics such as MTF, SNR, GIQE, NIIRS, and geolocation accuracy. For the SAR segment, the framework combines internal payload calibration, antenna calibration, corner-reflector-based verification, radiometric stability monitoring, and geolocation assessment using key SAR quality indicators including image resolution, radiometric performance, geolocation accuracy, PSLR, ISLR, ENL and NESZ. Together these activities provide end-to-end visibility of quality drivers and ensure the delivery of reliable EO products throughout mission lifetime.

b: The Earth observation community is increasingly looking to integrate commercial capabilities into legacy science archives. To do so, commercial data providers must aim to achieve the quality, uncertainty bounds, and consistency expected of flagship missions. To foster interoperability across these diverse platforms, international bodies such as the CEOS WGCV Infrared and Visible Optical Sensors (IVOS) Subgroup emphasize the need for standardized calibration specifications and the release of pre-launch parameters. A critical step in understanding this radiometric, spectral, and spatial data quality is ensuring sufficient system-level calibration and characterization prior to launch.

This paper will present a recommended set of prelaunch measurements for prospective instruments to assess data quality in alignment with the IVOS mission. Specifically, the guidance will outline recommendations across critical responsivity domains, including radiometric (e.g., linearity and signal-to-noise ratio), spectral (e.g., relative spectral response and out-of-band leakage), and spatial (e.g., modulation transfer function) characterizations. While the measurements themselves are fundamental to the assessment, detailed knowledge of the test methodologies, environments, and processes is equally essential to accurately quantifying measurement uncertainties. Adoption of these guidelines for prelaunch measurements by the remote sensing community will encourage the timely release of necessary pre-launch parameters and ensure that the integration of diverse sensor data preserves the scientific integrity of the global Earth observation record.

b: A Harmonised Cal/Val Framework for Hungary’s HUSAT Electro-Optical and SAR Constellation

The HUSAT Programme is developing Hungary’s space-based Earth observation capability through HULEO, comprising six very-high-resolution electro-optical (HUEOP) and two synthetic aperture radar (HUSAR) satellites. Because the two sensor families require different calibration methods, the challenge is to establish comparable and traceable confidence in both product families under common quality-assessment principles [1]. International calibration networks can provide a shared external reference basis for the two domains [2].

For HUEOP, our Cal/Val methodology will combine supplier evidence with external reference datasets and commercial georegistration sources [3], supplemented by a controlled Hungarian ground control point (GCP) network. This network will include surveyed optical targets treated as GCPs. Calibration GCPs and independent checkpoints will be separated, with controlled coordinates, uncertainty, validity and maintenance. Radiometric and spectral monitoring will use laboratory and field evidence, RadCalNet reference sites [4] and cross-sensor comparisons. The resulting quality evidence should be traceable and suitable for assessing product fitness for purpose [5].

For HUSAR, modality-specific indicators, methods and acceptance criteria must be defined independently, while evidence and uncertainty follow a structure comparable to HUEOP. Surveyed point targets can support independent SAR radiometric calibration [6] and geometric performance assessment [7]. CEOS SARCalNet resources could provide additional calibration sites and reference information for commissioning and long-term monitoring.

4iG Space and Defence participates in the SPHERE consortium, which is conducting a study for ESA on the evolution of the European Earth Observation ecosystem beyond 2040, including the integration and qualification of institutional, national and commercial EO capabilities [8]. The experience gained in SPHERE supports a common assessment logic for HUSAT’s modality-specific optical and SAR Cal/Val evidence. Alignment with ESA’s EDAP framework could provide a common basis for quality assessment across both modalities. Each metric should identify the applicable product, processing version, reference dataset and uncertainty. Potential ESA support includes method review, reference data and sites, uncertainty guidance, technical exchange and cross-calibration.

b: Reliable geometric validation of high-resolution Earth observation products requires consistent and dependable ground reference data. Geodetic metadata is at the core of the validation. Often occurring are differences in reference frames, coordinate epochs, height systems, and transformations. A dataset can still maintain high internal accuracy despite systematic offsets from the ground truth.

This presentation shows ways to address detected offsets and provides a practical framework built around five questions: intended use, reference system, required accuracy, supporting evidence, and independent assessment. It distinguishes projection changes from reference-frame transformations, examines coordinate epoch and crustal motion. Finally, independent checkpoints help to distinguish and eliminate geodetic inconsistencies from other error sources.

The workflow of transformations and projections is shown. It supports reproducible accuracy assessments and clearer communication between data providers, satellite operators, and product users. It will help reviewing metadata, proper coordinate testing, and documentation of conclusions and limitations.

b: Emerging certification frameworks for Earth Observation data rest on an assumption that is quietly failing: that a chain of custody exists, rooted in downlinked raw data that can be retrieved, reprocessed and independently audited. Increasingly it cannot be. Onboard edge processing now produces detections, cues, classifications and derived products in flight, and for reasons of bandwidth, tactical latency or data policy the Level 0 product is frequently never downlinked at all. When the raw phase history or full-frame imagery does not exist on the ground, the operative questions — is this product traceable, is it reproducible, can it be certified — have no current answer. Two developments compound the problem. Machine learning has become part of the measurement chain rather than an interpretation layer applied afterwards: a learned detection is a function of model architecture, weights, and training distribution as much as of photons, and reproducing it requires all three. And proliferation has made campaign-based audit arithmetically impossible, since the multi-month characterisation appropriate to one flagship instrument does not scale to fleets launched continuously. This contribution proposes a taxonomy and a candidate framework. We first argue that four distinct properties are routinely conflated in discussion of data veracity, and that they require different mechanisms. Authenticity — did this product originate from the sensor and processing chain it claims — and integrity — has it been altered since — are cryptographic problems, and are tractable. Accuracy — is this a correct measurement of the physical world — and fitness for purpose — is it sufficient for a stated use — are metrological problems, and are not. The central observation is that no amount of cryptographic assurance produces accuracy. A perfectly signed, perfectly unaltered product from a miscalibrated or degraded sensor is authentic, has integrity, and is wrong. Certification schemes that address only the first two properties will certify products that are demonstrably false, and will do so with high confidence. We then propose five mechanisms spanning both categories. Signing at the sensor, using a hardware root of trust, binds product, timestamp, platform state vector and processing version at the point of formation rather than at the ground segment. Model and weights pinning cryptographically binds algorithm state to output, making a learned product reproducible in principle even where its input was not retained. Statistically sampled raw downlink preserves an audit capability at manageable cost, with the sampling rate itself becoming a certifiable parameter of the system. Onboard uncertainty propagation allows uncertainty to travel with the product rather than being reconstructed on the ground from metadata that may no longer be sufficient. And attestation acquisitions — scheduled observations of a physical reference whose state is commanded, telemetered and independently known — provide a challenge-response demonstration that the entire chain, including the onboard processing and the learned components, remains unmodified and correctly calibrated. This last mechanism is the bridge between the cryptographic and

metrological halves of the problem, and it requires physical reference infrastructure of a kind the author addresses in a companion contribution. The framework draws on operational practice from intelligence-community source integration, where provenance, source characterisation and confidence annotation for non-traditional and commercial sensor data have been handled at scale for two decades, and where the distinction between a trusted source and a correct measurement is long established. We identify which of those practices are transferable to QA4EO and to an emerging civil certification scheme, and which are not. This is a framework contribution and not a results paper; no implementation is presented. It is offered to open discussion in a topic area this workshop has newly and deliberately created.

b: Earth Observation calibration infrastructure is organized by modality. RadCalNet and LANDHYPERNET address optical radiometry, TIRCalNet addresses thermal, SARCalNet and reference reflector arrays address radar, and ground control point and DEM validation frameworks address geometry. Each maintains distinct targets, distinct sites and distinct uncertainty budgets. Consequently there is no traceable answer to a question on which multi-sensor fusion products, CEOS-ARD interoperability claims, AI-derived products and emerging certification frameworks all depend: is a SAR-derived three-dimensional reconstruction geometrically and radiometrically consistent with a LIDAR point cloud and a photogrammetric reconstruction of the same scene, and to what stated uncertainty? The first-order obstacle is physical rather than algorithmic. Modalities cannot be registered against an object that does not exist in all of them. A checkerboard design installed on low-density, non-metalic, dry material can serve as an excellent optical resolution target and a radar null; a machined trihedral is an excellent radar reference and a poor optical texture target; textile-based, three-dimensional structures can yield a clean LIDAR point cloud and no radar return whatsoever. A predecessor effort to establish a combined optical, radar and three-dimensional reference site, in which the author participated, failed for exactly this reason: targets fabricated with textiles and other low-density materials were destroyed by severe weather and were, in any case, transparent at radar frequencies. Cross-modal reference design is therefore a materials and coatings problem before it is a geometry problem, and the resulting array must be simultaneously radar-opaque with predictable scattering, spectrally characterized in the visible and near-infrared, of known and stable emissivity in the thermal infrared, dimensionally stable, and weather-survivable. Three developments make this issue of importance. First, proliferation has broken the economics of per-sensor characterization: multi-month campaigns appropriate to a single flagship instrument do not scale to fleets of tens or hundreds of satellites launched continuously, and calibration throughput is becoming a constraint on operational availability rather than a preparatory activity. The same pressure applies to machine-learning products, where transferring a model trained on one sensor to another requires a traceable statement of how the two differ — an inter-sensor characterization problem that a common physical reference is uniquely positioned to answer — and where validating learned detection, classification and super-resolution products requires ground truth of known uncertainty rather than merely of known appearance. Second, dual-frequency missions such as NISAR require demonstration that L-band and S-band channels share a common geolocation and phase-center reference, which no single-band target can provide. Third, forthcoming bistatic and multistatic missions including ESA's Harmony have no adequate reference infrastructure, because conventional reflector arrays are monostatic by construction and a trihedral's bistatic radar cross-section is not its monostatic value. This contribution presents the design of a full cross-modal reference array together with the construction and characterization of an initial demonstrator subset. We distinguish throughout between measured results, completed design, and roadmap concept; no satellite calibration campaign results are presented. SHEEPFOLD extends the canonical-primitive philosophy established by the Sandia SLICY target under the DARPA/AFRL MSTAR program — in which scattering mechanisms are analytically predictable rather than merely surveyed — across the optical, thermal and three-dimensional domains. The choice of foundation is not strictly historical. The primitives Sandia selected for analytic tractability in electromagnetics — sphere, cylinder, plate, dihedral, trihedral, top-hat — are substantially the same primitives that three-dimensional point-cloud processing fits analytically. A cylinder's axis and radius are independently estimable in closed form from a SAR image and from a LIDAR point cloud; the difference between those two estimates, with its uncertainty, is the measurement this array exists to make. The array comprises extended-bottom-plate trihedrals and dihedrals as a multi-band ladder spanning X through L, the sizing of which is dictated by the λ⁻² scaling of reflector radar cross-section; metallic spheres of graduated radii providing a frequency-independent analytic cross-section ladder whose bistatic pattern is computable from Mie theory, making them the only tractable reference class for bistatic geometries and the correct reference for inter-channel balance in multi-band and sub-banded systems; extended three-dimensional structures — vertical and horizontal cylinders, rectangular volumes, and towers of varied height providing layover and shadow diversity — fabricated in materials selected and coated for simultaneous multi-modal response; optical resolution, edge and reflectance targets co-located with and mechanically referenced to the radar primitives rather than sited separately; and actively controlled instrumented blackbody plates. Each element carries an embedded instrumentation node supplying continuous, GNSS-disciplined, timestamped characterization of its own state and local environment: traceable thermometry with across-element gradient characterization; downwelling sky radiance, without which the reflected-radiance term for any non-unity-emissivity surface cannot be closed; atmospheric state, surface wetness, spectral irradiance and aerosol optical depth; concurrent in-band radio-frequency interference monitoring; and continuous pose by dual-antenna GNSS heading, inclinometry and inertial measurement. This instrumentation is required rather than optional. A reference claiming millimeter-class geometric traceability must account for its own thermomechanical state: aluminum structures of meter scale move by more than a millimeter across a typical diurnal cycle, dissimilar

materials within a composite element produce differential motion and therefore pose change, and thermal mass and coating emissivity jointly determine apparent temperature through the day. The target's geometry and radiometry are functions of its measured environment, not constants. Motorized elements self-orient to predicted overpass geometry from mission ephemeris and log achieved pose with the collection, enabling one installation to serve multiple missions and incidence angles without field intervention. These are throughput properties as much as metrological ones. Self-orientation removes the field intervention otherwise required per mission, machine-readable uncertainty-annotated output removes per-campaign manual processing, and a transportable standardized unit is replicable in quantity: proliferated constellations require proliferated references. The array is tiered so that the passive reference layer remains fully valid independent of the instrumentation and actuation layers. We present the structure of a preliminary uncertainty budget per modality and for the cross-modal transformation, developed using the CoMet framework, identifying and bounding the dominant terms in each: for the thermal reference, the gradient between embedded thermometry and the radiating surface and the reflected sky-radiance term; for the radar reference, phase-center location and pose knowledge; for the optical reference, BRDF characterization and soiling; and for the cross-modal transformation, thermomechanical dimensional state together with the frequency- and polarization-dependent offset between radar phase center and the surface sampled by LIDAR and photogrammetry. Measured residuals between analytically predicted and measured radar cross-section for the demonstrator primitives are reported against this framework. Because the array is transportable and self-orienting, it additionally functions as a transfer standard in the metrological sense: a common characterized artifact relocatable between established reference sites to measure site-to-site bias directly, rather than inferring it statistically through satellite observation, which entangles site bias with sensor behavior. As a roadmap concept, BELLWETHER would extend the approach to orbit. Its primary users are not nadir-pointing Earth observation missions, for which the observing geometry is unfavorable, but ground-based space surveillance radars and optical sensors — for which a known-cross-section object in a known orbit is the only means of absolute calibration at operational range, following the ODERACS precedent — and the emerging class of space-based inspection, rendezvous and space-domain-awareness sensors, which presently has no calibration infrastructure of any kind. Band selection follows this user set, spanning L and S, relevant to European and United States space surveillance radars including GESTRA and Space Fence, through X. Inflatable rigidizable spheres provide large, aspect-independent, analytically exact low-frequency references requiring no attitude control, with the achievable frequency ceiling set by surface figure: by the Ruze relation, approximately 9 mm RMS supports 1 dB efficiency loss at L-band and approximately 26 mm at P-band, tolerances compatible with inflatable construction, while X-band and precision optical geometry require rigid machined primitives. A specular sphere of known radius and reflectance simultaneously constitutes an optical point source of computable radiance requiring no onboard power, providing radar and optical references co-registered by construction. Optical

brightness is addressed through scheduled-only source activation, published ephemeris and coordination with the astronomical community; low-altitude placement provides natural disposal. Because both systems provide a commandable, telemetered reference of known state, they constitute a challenge-response trust anchor for product authentication, connecting directly to this workshop's certification and data veracity theme. Reference measurements will be published in machine-readable, uncertainty-annotated form consistent with established fiducial reference measurement conventions. We propose SHEEPFOLD and BELLWETHER as candidate community reference assets — commercially developed and operated, with reference measurements published openly, and with requirements developed in coordination with CEOS WGCV. This contribution opens that requirements-gathering process.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Alia Khan<sup>1</sup>, Colby Rand<sup>1</sup>
b: Snow algae are microscopic organisms that act as light-absorbing particles on snow and ice surfaces, reducing surface albedo and accelerating snowmelt by as much as 40% through a bio-albedo feedback loop. Accurately mapping the spatial and temporal distribution of snow algae is therefore critical for understanding their role in cryosphere dynamics. However, traditional government-operated satellite platforms such as Landsat and Sentinel-2 are limited by their coarse spatial resolution, which prevents reliable delineation of fine-scale algae blooms.

This study evaluates the capabilities of commercial satellite imagery—SkySat, PlanetScope, BlackSky, and WorldView—acquired through NASA's Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) program, for detecting and mapping a recurring red snow algae bloom on the Mazama Glacier of Mt. Baker, Washington. A key challenge identified during evaluation is that commercial satellites lack a shortwave infrared (SWIR) band, preventing calculation of the Normalized Difference Snow Index (NDSI)—the most reliable method for isolating snow-covered areas prior to algae classification. Blue-band thresholding was applied as an alternative but was found to be less accurate, especially in shadowed or high-albedo terrain. Additionally, PlanetScope imagery acquired in spring and early summer exhibited extensive oversaturation artifacts caused by the high reflectivity of snow, rendering many of those images unsuitable for analysis; only late July through September acquisitions were usable. Classification of red snow algae further required sensor-specific threshold tuning of spectral indices.

Despite these limitations, commercial satellites demonstrate clear advantages for snow algae mapping. SkySat's 0.5 m/pixel resolution—the highest available among multispectral Earth-observing satellites—enables precise delineation of bloom boundaries and fine-scale spatial patterns not resolvable by government-funded sensors. This study confirms that, with sensor-appropriate threshold calibration and careful screening for oversaturation, commercial satellites accessed through CSDA provide a powerful new capability for high-resolution, high-frequency monitoring of snow algae and their contributions to cryosphere change.

b: The Spanish Component of the Atlantic Constellation (ESCA) is a strategic national initiative led by the Spanish Space Agency (AEE) and implemented by the European Space Agency (ESA). The system is conceived to complement existing EO programmes by delivering rapid, cost-effective, multi-sensor data, with twice-daily revisit of any location across Spain, Portugal and their respective Exclusive Economic Zones.

ESCA is an end-to-end space system built around four elements: a constellation of eight identical small satellites; a Flight Operations Segment (FOS); a Payload Data Ground Segment (PDGS); and a secure Marketplace for user access and mission tasking. Each spacecraft carries a VHR multispectral imager, a GNSS-R payload, an AIS receiver and an IoT payload. Together, these instruments support a wide range of applications, including land monitoring, agriculture, maritime surveillance and emergency response.

Our presentation addresses the optical payload and the ground-based activities that will guarantee and enable assessment of the quality of its data products. It describes the PDGS processing chain, from the acquisition of raw data to the generation of calibrated, geolocated products ready for users. It will also introduce the nominal calibration and validation (Cal/Val) strategy adopted for the mission, covering in-orbit activities. Finally, it defines the key parameters and performance metrics to be monitored to assess the optical payload's performance, such as radiometric accuracy, spatial resolution, and geolocation accuracy, ensuring that the data meet the requirements of the mission and its end users. Additional information on the engagement of Spanish cal/val networks will also be provided.

b: Accurate localization of field-measured ground control points (GCPs) in remote sensing imagery is essential for geometric calibration, validation, and accuracy assessment. However, automated localization remains challenging because field photographs and overhead remote sensing images differ substantially in scale, viewpoint, resolution, and imaging modality. This study presents an AI-based framework for automatically transferring field-measured GCPs to National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP) imagery. Rather than directly matching individual field photographs with NAIP images, multiple field images acquired around a GCP are integrated using AI and computer vision techniques to reconstruct the local scene and generate a local orthoimage. The precise GCP location is identified in the local orthoimage, which is subsequently matched with NAIP imagery to determine the corresponding image coordinates. A large language model (LLM) is further employed to describe the localized GCP and its surrounding environment, providing semantic information for interpretation and quality control. The framework was evaluated using hundreds of GCPs and thousands of field images collected across multiple U.S. states and diverse environments. Most field GCPs can be processed automatically with a localization uncertainty of approximately one pixel. As an additional outcome, the localized GCPs provide independent reference measurements for assessing NAIP geometric accuracy, showing that its positional accuracy is typically better than 1 m. The results demonstrate the potential of integrating AI, computer vision, and large language model for scalable and reliable field-to-image GCP localization and description.

b: Globally, the need to accurately measure water in rivers, lakes and reservoirs has never been greater. Floods and droughts are among the most impactful of natural hazards, causing billions of Euros of damage and claiming thousands of lives every year. Our planet's rapidly changing climate is intensifying both of these phenomena. Geopolitical tensions can also heighten the need to understand water availability and hazards with great accuracy and timeliness.
In this context, effective measurements and observations of water as both a resource and a threat are essential, but are sadly lacking.

This presentation explores the potential of very high-resolution earth observing satellites and low-cost aerial drones to deliver transformational change to the observation and management of of water and water related threats globally. A particular emphasis will be placed on prospects for improving observations of the speed of flow of water in times of extreme flooding using optical, thermal and synthetic aperture radar sensing capabilities.
Finally, there will be a call to the community to join efforts to develop solutions to this wicked problem for remote sensing of rivers.

b: VICALOPS is the European Space Agency's (ESA) new service dedicated to monitoring the radiometric performance of satellite sensors. It integrates various vicarious calibration methods that leverage reflectance from bright desert surfaces, snow, deep convective clouds (DCC), atmospheric molecules, and sunglint. The system synthesizes results by combining data from these methods to provide a comprehensive overview of sensor calibration and stability.

The calibration techniques implemented within VICALOPS have been thoroughly tested and validated using the DIMITRI toolbox on a variety of satellite data, with detailed error assessments carried out to ensure accuracy. VICALOPS currently supports the following sensors, starting from their first post-launch acquisition: MODIS (Terra and Aqua), VIIRS, Landsat 8 and 9, Sentinel-2/MSI (A, B and C), Sentinel-3/SLSTR (A and B), Sentinel-3/OLCI (A and B), EarthCARE/MSI, FLEX and historical sensors such as MERIS, VEGETATION, ATSR2/AATSR, and PARASOL. However, there are no limitations, and the service can be extended to integrate new commercial small sensors upon request and subject to agreement.

The service has been enhanced to efficiently handle the increasing volume of data and results, with several million results now managed within the SQL database. The underlying data management and processing capabilities have been upgraded to ensure scalability and efficient access to these large datasets.

The service is close to being opened to expert users, with only a few remaining details to be finalized, such as adding quick views of the latest available data and the most recent results and synthesis.

b: The STARWELL Small Satellite Calibration Facility (SSCF) is a pre-flight calibration facility providing SI-traceable spectral radiance calibration across the ultraviolet, visible, and short-wave infrared (UV-vis-SWIR) spectral regions. Developed by the UK's National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in partnership with STFC RAL Space, STARWELL was established to provide easy access to low-uncertainty SI-traceable radiometric calibration for the rapidly expanding small satellite and commercial Earth observation sector.

Located at the RAL Space campus in Harwell, Oxfordshire, the STARWELL facility combines a large-area integrating sphere, fed by both QTH lamps and a 1 kHz pulsed tuneable laser, with a novel SI-traceable reference detector and a spectrometer. This enables radiometric calibration measurements from 350 nm to 2500 nm with both monochromatic and broadband sources. In accordance with internationally recognised guidelines for calibration of optical remote-sensing instruments [1], these measurements establish a traceable baseline of instrument performance under controlled conditions, enabling robust uncertainty quantification and providing a reference against which in-orbit performance and long-term stability can be assessed. Through a fully documented uncertainty chain linked to internationally recognised primary standards, STARWELL supports the principles of measurement traceability and comparability promoted by the Quality Assurance Framework for Earth Observation (QA4EO) [2], ensuring interoperability across sensors, missions, and timescales.

Since commissioning in April 2025, STARWELL has supported a range of commercial and operational Earth observation programmes. These include radiometric calibration transfer for facilities supporting a flagship Copernicus mission, together with pre-flight radiometric calibration of payloads for two commercial small satellite operators, one of which is a Copernicus Contributing Mission.

This presentation will provide an overview of the STARWELL facility, its performance validation, measurement capabilities, and early operational use. Through recent calibration case studies, it will highlight the facility's capability to deliver SI-traceable radiometric calibration for both emerging NewSpace operators and established satellite programmes. The presentation will also discuss how STARWELL aligns with evolving community best practices for instrument calibration in remote-sensing [3], supporting the growing demand for high-quality Earth observation data across scientific, environmental, and commercial applications.

b: Hyperspectral imaging systems require the joint characterization of spectral, radiometric, spatial, and detector performance. However, calibration is commonly performed through separate test procedures, fixed acquisition grids, and independently estimated performance indicators. This fragmented approach does not fully account for parameter correlations, measurement uncertainty, model identifiability, or differences in the information content and cost of candidate experiments. Consequently, conventional characterization campaigns may oversample similar wavelengths, illumination levels, exposure times, or field positions, while still failing to separate correlated instrument effects and adequately constrain system-level performance quantities.

This work introduces HyperSpecs-OED, a model-driven framework for hyperspectral camera characterization based on Optimal Experimental Design. Before an acquisition is performed, the framework estimates how much information it is expected to provide about unknown spectral, radiometric, detector, and spatial-response parameters. Using a Fisher-information approximation, it evaluates how strongly the predicted measurement changes with those parameters relative to its expected uncertainty and therefore predicts how much the acquisition could improve their estimation. This uncertainty is propagated from the model parameters to user-defined performance quantities, including spectral center and bandwidth, throughput, photo-response non-uniformity, dark current, read noise, spectral smile, and spatial-resolution metrics. Candidate measurements are then selected sequentially according to characterization targets, acquisition cost, and feasibility constraints.

Although primarily intended for laboratory and on-ground characterization campaigns, the framework is fully configurable in terms of instrument model, measurement procedures, uncertainty assumptions, performance targets, and experimental constraints.

The resulting experimental plan specifies which measurements should be performed and under which operating conditions, including spectral channels and field positions, wavelength and illumination setpoints, integration times, frame counts, and spatial-target configurations. Its performance is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations by comparing a mandatory pilot campaign with the same campaign augmented by the optimized acquisition sequence. Shared multi-stage processing pipelines ensure consistency among raw-data simulation, experimental data reduction, model fitting, and uncertainty evaluation. A numerical case study applies HyperSpecs-OED to the joint characterization of a compact hyperspectral camera across multiple spectral channels and locations across the field of view. The candidate campaign includes wavelength scans, dark and flat-field measurements, and slanted-edge images. These data are linked through a common forward model to estimate spectral response and smile, radiometric throughput, conversion gain, PRNU, dark current, read noise, and directional MTF. Spectral response is inferred from the measured detector signal while accounting for the finite bandwidth of the illumination source, whereas MTF is extracted from simulated raw images through a complete slanted-edge processing pipeline. The proposed approach therefore provides a unified and traceable route from physical camera modelling to uncertainty-aware experiment selection, enabling hyperspectral characterization campaigns that are more informative, efficient, and directly aligned with system-level performance requirements.

b: The growing capability of high-resolution Earth Observation (EO) systems to detect, localise and quantify methane point sources is creating a corresponding need for independent ground-based observations suitable for product validation and intercomparison. This is particularly challenging for real industrial sources, where emissions may originate from multiple locations and vary substantially over timescales comparable with, or shorter than, two consecutive satellite overpasses.

In this context, the potential role of ground-based scanning Tunable Diode LiDAR (TD-LiDAR) as a complementary component of methane Cal/Val activities is explored. Unlike point measurements or temporally aggregated facility estimates, a spatially scanning TD-LiDAR, being a remote devise, can repeatedly observe the spatial distribution of atmospheric methane enhancements over a facility, localise emitting areas and, when combined with local wind information, support sourcelevel emission-rate estimation. Continuous acquisitions can therefore provide information not only on the magnitude of an emission, but also on its persistence and temporal evolution, providing additional information that could support and complement Leak Detection and Repair (LDAR) program.

This approach builds on operational experience acquired within the BioMethane Tracer project, cofunded by the Emilia-Romagna PR FESR 2021–2027, where TD-LiDAR was deployed continuously for approximately 338 h over three seasonal campaigns at 4 different operating anaerobic digestion facilities. The instrument was used together with complementary in-situ measurement techniques and source-specific estimation approaches to characterise the facilitywide emission environment. The campaigns highlighted the coexistence of persistent, intermittent and short-duration methane emissions and showed that both emission intensity and the relative contribution of individual sources may vary markedly with time and operating conditions.

The observations performed within the BioMethane Tracer project suggest a possible application of spatially resolved scanning TD-LiDAR measurements to support satellite methane product validation. Continuous ground-based observations acquired before, during and after a satellite overpass could characterise the methane emission state of the facility at the time of observation. This temporal context could help determine whether differences between satellite and groundbased estimates arise from the measurement methods or from actual changes in the emitting sources.

Rather than replacing established reference approaches such as controlled releases, continuous scanning TD-LiDAR observations could complement them by extending Cal/Val activities to temporally variable, multi-source industrial environments. Coordinated satellite and ground-based experiments including TD-LiDAR could help assess measurement comparability and uncertainty in methane EO validation.

https://earth.esa.int/documents/d/earth-.a: Nicolas Misk<sup>2</sup>, Vincent Leroy<sup>1</sup>, Claudia Emde<sup>1</sup>, Yves Govaerts<sup>1</sup>, Marta Luffarelli<sup>1</sup>
b: Accurate ground-based measurements of surface reflectance are essential for the calibration and validation of satellite Earth observation products. Fiducial Reference Measurements (FRM) represent the highest standard for such measurements, requiring full uncertainty characterization, traceability, and independence to ensure reliable sensor validation. Such measurements are commonly performed using spectroradiometers mounted on aircraft or Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) operating in the lower atmosphere. A key source of uncertainty in these measurements arises from atmospheric diffuse illumination, which is often assumed to be isotropic. These uncertainties can propagate through calibration chains, affecting the reliability of long-term satellite observation records and climate monitoring activities for instance. We quantify the error introduced by this isotropy assumption on the measured reflectance using a set of 3D scenes simulated with the Eradiate radiative transfer model.

Spectroradiometers measure radiance reflected by the surface of interest within a narrow field of view; the measured surface spectral properties are described by the Hemispherical-Directional Reflectance Factor (HDRF). We simulate and compare HDRF computed using isotropic and anisotropic measurement equations on a selection of four explicit 3D scenes. The scenes include a patch of uniform, 6cm high grass (case A), a collection of orchard tree rows (case B), and a forested area reconstructed from Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) techniques and acquired in both winter and summer conditions (cases C and D).

The simulated vegetation acts as a source of anisotropy in the downwelling radiance field through multiple scattering. Surface spectral properties vary from one scene to another, and observations are performed at four spectral bands in the visible range.

We show that accounting for the inherently anisotropic diffuse downwelling radiance effects in the visible domain is essential. Biases between results simulated with each of the two measurement equations are sensitive to the solar zenith angle (SZA) and aerosol optical depth (AOD). Even under favorable simulated conditions (SZA=15° and AOD = 0.1), isotropy is an uncertainty source which can introduce a systematic bias at 460nm ranging from 3.07%±6.20% to 10.46%±1.84%, relative to anisotropic HDRF estimates. Observed bias variations across test cases (from <10% to >20%) are difficult to accurately predict based on the atmospheric, measurement and illumination conditions. Biases are correlated with higher viewing and solar zenith angles, higher AOD, and the most complex 3D scenes (cases C and D). When reported to the total uncertainty budget defined for the MODIS and subsequent Sentinel-2A land products, the biases introduced reach a significant percentage of the allowed error margin and exceed it for scene C.

The isotropy assumption introduces errors that are significant compared to the latest CEOS WGCV recommendations of 5% for in-situ measurements. This highlights significant limitations of the isotropy-based approaches, especially when producing FRMs. Furthermore, this study examines only a subset of the potential error sources, as the test cases exclude additional anisotropy sources such as a ground elevation gradient and the presence of clouds in the vicinity of the measurements. To overcome these limitations associated with surface reflectance characterization, we propose as part of the ESA FRM4VEG project a new protocol for surface reflectance retrievals based on an artificial target with known reflective properties (THEMIS). THEMIS would allow us to accurately evaluate new surface retrieval methods for in-situ measurements that account for diffuse radiance anisotropy.

b: NASA has procured 5 Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instruments to collect radiance and reflectance measurements in support of scientific research, rapid response, weather and climate applications. All 5 instruments have gone through pre-launch ground tests to calibrate and characterize spectral, radiometric and geometric performance, and 3 of them are currently in on-orbit operations. This poster focuses on the tests on sensor (detector) spatial responses. The responses are measured by line spread functions in the along-scan and along-track directions. The presentation will highlight lessons learned from VIIRS pre-launch tests, including anomalies observed across optical, thermal, and electronic design/fabrication that varied from build to build, and the corresponding improvements implemented to mitigate these issues.

b: Post-launch calibration and validation of satellite instruments is needed to enable measurements from different satellites to be inter-compared and used seamlessly together. To help address this need we have established a set of automated validation sites where the necessary measurements for validating mid and thermal infrared data from spaceborne and airborne sensors are made every few minutes on a continuous basis.

The locations of the validation sites include Lake Tahoe CA/NV, Salton Sea CA, and Russell Ranch CA, which have been operating for multiple decades as well as several new US and international sites. Each site includes one of the JPL developed radiometers together with other instrumentation provided by the validation site operators. A full list of sites is available on the calval website (https://calval.jpl.nasa.gov). The JPL radiometers are custom-built, highly accurate (50mK) radiometers measuring the surface skin temperature. Data from the sites are being used to help validate data products from commercial mid and thermal infrared sensors as part of the NASA Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program. This presentation will include an update on the CSDA program together with recent results using data from the sites to validate mid and thermal infrared data products from satellite-sensor systems.

b: NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program has acquired a plethora of high-resolution earth observation data. The relationship between the size of each pixel’s footprint on the ground and the space between adjacent pixel centers is an important aspect of every observation. These metrics can be measured with the MTF (Modulation Transfer Function) and the FWHM (Full-Width at Half Maximum) of the LSF (Line Spread Function). Here we present preliminary results of down-sampling data from PlanetScope’s SuperDove sensors. These sensors provide data spaced every 3m but the FWHM of the LSF is ~9m (3 pixels) with an MTF at Nyquist frequency of ~0.1%. We show preliminary results of various methods of down-sampling this data to 9m pixel spacing. To perform this down-sampling, currently 4 different 3x3 aggregation kernels are tested. The first aggregation scheme is a simple subsampling of the data, achieved by using a 3x3 rectangular kernel with a 1 original resolution pixel FWHM. This produces down-sampled data with a FWHM of ~11m (1.2 pixels) with MTF at Nyquist of ~32%. We also tested with a 3x3 rectangular kernel with FWHM of 3 (original resolution) pixels, producing down-sampled data with a FWHM of ~12m (1.4 pixels) with MTF at Nyquist of ~24%. A gaussian 3x3 kernel with FWHM of 1 (original resolution) pixel was also tested and produced down-sampled data with a FWHM of ~11m (1.2 pixels) with MTF at Nyquist of ~27%. The final kernel tested uses a circularly rotated triangular weighting (resembling a tent) with a FWHM of 1 (original resolution) pixel and produces down-sampled data with a FWHM of ~12m (1.3 pixels) with MTF at Nyquist of ~26%. Down-sampling of PlanetScope data brings about compatibility between the pixel spacing and footprint size, while simultaneously improving MTF to an image quality comparable to those available from public optical sensors.

b: Long-term radiometric consistency of reflflective solar bands in satellite sensors is essential for quantitative remote sensing, yet conventional vicarious calibration is constrained by the limited availability and diversity of large homogeneous calibration sites. This study proposes a global pseudo-invariant pixel (GPIP)-based method for instrument response tracking and cross-calibration. GPIPs are identifified from long-term multispectral image pairs over nine global regions using the iteratively reweighted multivariate alteration detection (IR-MAD) method, providing numerous calibration samples across diverse surface types and a broad reflflectance range. The resulting GPIPs are applied to long time series FY-3D MERSI-II observations to estimate long-term radiometric response degradation. The derived trends are consistent across regions and agree with those obtained using traditional vicarious calibration methods. A preliminary analysis is also conducted for Sentinel-3 OLCI, including radiometric response degradation assessment and PIP-based cross-calibration with MERSI. Together, these applications demonstrate the potential of PIPs as a sensor-independent reference for frequent radiometric response monitoring and cross-calibration of reflflective solar bands.

b: Non-Uniformity Correction (NUC) of HotSat imagery is a two-step process, where high spatial frequency (detector pixel-to-pixel variability) non-uniformity is assessed using images of the onboard blackbody calibrators and low spatial frequencies (vignetting, narcissus, instrument self-emission) are estimated from flat-field images of uniform ocean targets.

In particular, if left uncorrected, variations in instrument self-emission introduce up to 8 K gradients across a given frame. Such levels of uncertainty have the potential to dominate the signal from measurements seeking to determine changes in temperature of many industrial assets over time. Therefore, improvements in the NUC algorithm have a large beneficial impact in the value of HotSat images for time series analyses.

In this work we present methods and algorithms developed to perform non-uniformity correction for the HotSat instrument and show how recent improvements have enabled the detection of smaller variations in assets temperatures (both temporally and spatially).

b: Planet has been successfully leveraging lunar captures for calibration and validation purposes with the Planetscope constellation, since 2016. In this work, we explore lunar calibrations for Tanager-1, which carries an imaging spectrometer whose radiometric and spatial calibration is conventionally tracked against terrestrial targets. Complementing lunar radiometric calibration, this poster presents two methods that use the dark and high-contrast structure of the same acquisitions. First, we use deep-space regions within lunar captures to validate routine darkfield collections. Daily darkfield calibration currently relies on night-time collects over dark ocean, which may be contaminated by atmospheric traces, terrestrial light sources such as ships and islands, and lunar stray light. Deep space provides a true zero-radiance baseline against which these night-ocean darkfields can be benchmarked while taking lunar stray light into account. Second, we estimate Tanager sharpness from the lunar limb. Standard sharpness tracking relies on terrestrial bridge targets, which are limited by atmospheric interference, variable target upkeep, in-scene clutter, and competition with commercial tasking. The Moon presents a high-contrast, atmosphere-free edge, requires no maintenance, and is available on demand, enabling reliable Relative Edge Response (RER) estimation across all bands from a single acquisition, while taking into account the thermal environment for imaging. We describe how limb curvature, libration and phase angle, and lunar-pointing acquisition geometry are accounted for, and compare the resulting RER. Together these off-Earth techniques overcome the limitations of ground targets and support robust radiometric and spatial calibration of Tanager imagery.

b: Assessing the on-orbit performance of nighttime thermal imagery requires more than a single metric. Radiometric accuracy, geometric performance, noise, and spatial resolution together determine the quality and usability of the resulting data.

This work presents nighttime calibration and validation activities for Hydrosat's VanZyl thermal imaging missions. Radiometric performance is assessed using independent ground and satellite references, including NOAA and SURFRAD measurements and coincident observations from established Earth-observation missions. Geometric performance is evaluated using reference imagery to characterize geolocation and registration accuracy.

Beyond conventional Cal/Val, we examine the practical challenges of deriving image-quality metrics from nighttime on-orbit imagery. MTF estimates from thermal features such as coastlines and bridges can depend strongly on target selection, thermal contrast, edge geometry, sampling, and scene variability. Similar considerations affffect estimates of image noise when natural targets are used.

These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating radiometric, geometric, and spatial performance together. Lessons from the VanZyl missions are being used to develop repeatable performance-monitoring approaches for Hydrosat's upcoming thermal imaging constellation.

b: The Digital Twin Earth Synthetic Scene Generator and Observation Simulator (DTE-S2GOS) is a novel pre-operational service integrated within the Destination Earth (DestinE) platform of the European Space Agency (ESA). DTE-S2GOS produces a “radiative twin” of Earth: physically realistic 3-D synthetic scenes of terrestrial environments and the corresponding simulated observations as captured by ground- or space-based remote-sensing instruments. Utilising the Eradiate radiative-transfer model, the framework supports multiple spatial scales, from sub metre-level representations of ground observations to kilometre-scale global landscapes suited for atmospheric or climate-scale studies.

Demonstration use-cases, such as synthetic satellite observations for new missions like CHIME illustrate value for algorithm testing, satellite calibration/validation, and ML training. Planned scientific validation includes comparisons with real satellite/ground-based data from reference networks (e.g. HYPERNETS, RadCalNet), using rigorous uncertainty propagation workflows. Practical examples of ground observation and satellite simulation will be provided for the Gobabeb HYPERNETS and San Rossore ICOS sites. The impacts of ground observation environments such as mast or tower will be illustrated. Finally, assumption behind upscaling methods will be quantified.

DTE-S2GOS contributes a critical “synthetic observation” component to the broader DTE ecosystem, enhancing flexibility and complementarity across Digital Twin efforts. By providing high-fidelity simulated EO data and bridging modelling with applied workflows, it supports ESA’s ambition to build robust, interoperable Earth-system digital twins — and helps the community explore a wide range of what-if scenarios for environment, climate and land-use change.

b: NASA CSDA evaluates in-flight Sensor Spatial Resolution from images ranging in pixel size from 0.3 m to 100 m. This poster gives a detailed explanation of the process at varying pixel sizes, intended for clarity in the evaluation process as well as for use by others to perform the same evaluation. The process is covered from the initial extraction of pixels along a knife edge, construction of edge spread function (ESF) and line spread function (LSF), all the way through modulation transfer function (MTF) calculation and determination of the metrics we use for our spatial resolution evaluation. Our methods for extracting LSF from images of bridges as well as when and how to account for bridge width impacts are discussed in detail as well. Relative Edge Response (RER), Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) and MTF at Nyquist are explained and categorized in the rankings of best to worst: Ideal, Excellent, Good, and Basic. Code samples in python will also be displayed.

b: The rapid expansion of satellite-based methane (CH₄) monitoring has highlighted the need for harmonized, transparent, and evidence-based validation approaches. While the recent methane plume initiatives (EU-MARS and ESA-CAMS) have established a set of community-accepted common practices, the transition towards best practice requires quantitative evidence demonstrating how specific retrieval methods, assumptions, uncertainty treatments, and validation approaches improve product reliability and fitness-for-purpose.

This study explores how the EDAP+ Maturity Matrix can provide a structured framework to support this transition. The maturity-based approach enables systematic assessment of documentation, uncertainty characterization, validation evidence, metrological traceability, and product-generation methods, while identifying gaps and priorities for improvement.

Studies from the ESA MEDUSA and METRICS activities, together with US academic validation campaigns, shows the need for representative validation datasets covering a broad range of emission scenarios and environmental conditions, improved treatment of uncertainty contributors, and transparent performance comparison across different methodologies.

The EDAP+ Maturity Matrix is a practical pathway to bridge from common practice to best practice by introducing quantitative assessment criteria, evidence-based grading, and continuous improvement mechanisms. Such an approach can facilitate internationally accepted validation standards, improve comparability across methane missions and products, and increase confidence in satellite-derived methane emission estimates for scientific, operational, and regulatory applications.

b: The rapid advancement of hyperspectral imaging technology has rendered high-resolution spectral data indispensable for quantitative Earth observation applications. Conventional radiometric calibration approaches, however, are subject to inherent limitations: vicarious calibration necessitates concurrent field measurements, whereas cross-calibration is hampered by the paucity of stable hyperspectral reference sensors in orbit. To address these challenges, this paper presents a novel on-orbit radiometric calibration framework based on model-driven spectral reconstruction, which enables the calibration of hyperspectral sensors—exemplified by the Environmental Mapping and Analysis Program (EnMAP)—using well-calibrated multispectral sensors, such as Sentinel-2/MSI and MODIS, as reference standards. A comprehensive atmospheric sensitivity analysis reveals that water vapor content (WVC) introduces errors of up to 15% in water absorption bands, whereas aerosol optical depth at 550 nm (AOD@550 nm) exerts a negligible influence (less than 1%). In this study, the proposed method was implemented by employing MOD05_L2 WVC retrievals and setting AOD@550nm to a fixed value of 0.05 for EnMAP radiometric calibration. Validation was conducted over 27 EnMAP acquisitions spanning from the satellite's launch to December 31, 2024, over the Railroad Valley Playa (RVP) and Gobabeb test sites. The results demonstrate outstanding consistency with reflectance-based calibration, yielding relative errors below 5%, and maintain deviations of less than 10% relative to onboard calibration outcomes, even in the presence of sensor degradation. Collectively, these findings establish a robust alternative methodology for the radiometric calibration of space-borne hyperspectral sensors, particularly advantageous for those lacking dedicated onboard calibration subsystems.

b: In December 2025 and March 2026, the first two batches of the Eaglet-II multispectral CubeSat constellation were successfully launched. Eaglet-II represents a high-resolution optical imaging component of IRIDE, one of the most complex and comprehensive Earth Observation systems in the world. IRIDE is a "constellation of constellations" comprising SAR, hyperspectral, and multispectral satellites. Funded by Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), the IRIDE mission is coordinated by the European Space Agency (ESA) with support from the Italian Space Agency (ASI). Developed by OHB Italia, the Eaglet-II constellation is designed to provide rapid, high-resolution imagery to support a wide range of civilian, environmental, and infrastructure monitoring applications.

Eaglet-II features high-resolution optical imagers capable of acquiring RGB imagery covering an area of roughly 15km by 20km at a ground sampling distance of 2m. To guarantee a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio, the payload features a Time Delay Integration (TDI) mode with 15 stages. The satellites support two imaging modes, acquiring data in either spot (single image) or strip (multiple sequential images) mode. Following the launches, in-flight geometric calibration was executed in the first half of 2026 under the responsibility of OHB Italia with support from OHB System. The calibration workflow relies on a tool developed by OHB System featuring a fully automated processing chain. The tool automatically matches acquisitions with Sentinel-2 reference imagery to identify and process Ground Control Points for estimation of misalignment angles and focal length.

This presentation will provide an overview of Eaglet-II’s design, and we will detail the automated processing chain of the calibration tool and highlight some of its key features. Furthermore, we will share the first calibration results for selected satellites from both batches, demonstrating the excellent geometric performance achieved (CE90<30m). Lastly, we will discuss the future work, which focuses on further improving the geolocation accuracy with even higher resolution reference images.

b: Radio frequency interference (RFI) has emerged as a significant source of degradation in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, compromising the quality and reliability of downstream Earth observation applications. RFI-induced artifacts can degrade algorithmic performance, which leads to false detections in object localization techniques and increases the need for costly manual quality assessment. Although most existing RFI detection methods operate on computationally intensive raw or single-look complex products, we focus on the more practical task of detecting and localizing RFI directly in lightweight ground range detected quick-look images. In the ClearSAR challenge (https://platform-challenges.philab.esa.int/clear-sar), we introduced the first AI-ready benchmark for RFI detection in Sentinel-1 quick-look imagery. The benchmark includes quality-controlled annotations of real-world RFI artifacts, a standardized train-test split, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. To promote fair comparison and accelerate research in this area, we asked the community to develop new RFI detection algorithms within the ClearSAR (Track 1) challenge, held in conjunction with the IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (IEEE ICIP 2026). Overall, the challenge attracted 171 registered teams, with 120 actively submitting solutions throughout the challenge, enabling a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art RFI detection methods. In this talk, we will present the dataset used in the challenge, discuss the evaluation process for comparing the approaches developed in ClearSAR, and present the procedure followed to generate ground-truth RFI bounding boxes. We will discuss the three top-performing approaches and highlight the key findings and lessons learned from the competition. By providing an openly accessible dataset, a standardized evaluation framework, and a continuously available benchmark, ClearSAR establishes a reproducible foundation for advancing AI-based quality control of Sentinel-1 products and supports the development of robust RFI detection methods for operational Earth observation systems.
