b: On the Korean Peninsula, where rainfall is concentrated in the summer season, monitoring reservoirs as a source of available water is essential. However, most reservoirs in Korea remain ungauged, so satellite remote sensing, which can continuously monitor large areas, is an effective alternative for reservoir monitoring. Water body detection has conventionally relied on the 10 m resolution Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery provided by the European Space Agency (ESA). Because most Korean reservoirs are small in surface area with complex shorelines, this spatial resolution causes mixed pixels along water body boundaries and degrades detection performance. Accurate reservoir detection therefore requires imagery of higher spatial resolution. In this study, water body detection was performed using CAS500-1 (Compact Advanced Satellite 500-

imagery, a Korean high-resolution optical satellite providing 0.5 m panchromatic and 2.0 m multispectral bands. Deep learning based semantic segmentation models were trained on CAS500-1 imagery to extract water bodies over reservoirs in South Korea, and manually delineated water/non-water binary masks were used as reference data for accuracy assessment. Detection results were compared with those derived from 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery to quantify the improvement obtained from higher spatial resolution, with particular attention to boundary regions and small reservoirs. In addition, the extracted water surface areas were validated as a time series against in-situ reservoir storage records, and the performance of each AI technique was evaluated. The results indicate that that CAS500-1 imagery combined with AI-based segmentation enables accurate delineation of reservoir water bodies, including boundary areas where medium-resolution imagery is limited. This approach is expected to support more efficient water resource management for ungauged reservoirs in Korea.

b: The Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) is establishing gravel-based optical calibration and validation (cal/val) target sites in Korea. Test Target 1 (TT1), consisting of two 6×6 m2 white and black gravel targets, was established on a building rooftop in Daejeon in 2023. Test Target 2 (TT2), comprising three 15×15 m2 targets with high, middle, and low reflflectances, was established on reclaimed land at the Boseong Standard Meteorological Observatory in 2024. Test Target 3 (TT3), featuring three 15×15 m2 targets with high, medium, and low reflflectances, was constructed at the Goheung Aviation Center in 2026. Meteorological variables–including air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and direction, and solar radiation–were monitored on a tower inside the TT1. A sky radiometer (POM02, Prede) was installed at TT3 to retrieve aerosol optical depth (AOD) and precipitable water vapor (PWV). Additionally, two spectral radiometers (RoX) were installed at TT3 to continuously monitor the downward and upward spectral irradiance of the high- and low-reflflectance targets. Field campaigns were conducted to derive calibration offffsets and slopes for validating satellite signals. The results demonstrate that these test targets are suitable for optical satellites with spatial resolutions of a few meters or higher. KARI plans to establish four 30×30 m2 or larger gravel targets (high, medium-high, medium-low, and low reflflectance) to meet the requirements for optical satellites with spatial resolutions of 5–10 m or fifiner.

b: Cross-calibration between sensors allows the quantification of radiometric differences and establishes consistency across Earth observation missions in the same spectral domain. An established method is through simultaneous observations, but the identification, correction and uncertainty analysis of these matchups globally is challenging across diverse surfaces, atmospheric and viewing conditions. In addition, residual discrepancies may remain between sensor and reference observations after correcting for known effects, owing to imperfect characterisation and other factors that are difficult to model explicitly, motivating the investigation of complementary data-driven correction methods.

Developed within the ESA-funded Met4EO project, this work investigates how artificial intelligence can complement physics-based cross-calibration workflows through three complementary applications: automated region of interest (ROI) selection, scalable uncertainty-aware observation mismatch correction using radiative-transfer emulation, and data-driven modelling of residual radiometric discrepancies.

To identify suitable ROIs that are sufficiently homogeneous to support low uncertainty cross-calibration, we developed an unsupervised region-selection approach that combines DEM-based terrain filtering with k-means clustering of texture-derived features. Validation using simulated Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2 observations showed that the derived masks reduced heterogeneity-driven variability while preserving mean sensor agreement without introducing systematic bias.

While automated ROI selection increases matchup availability, scalable correction of observation mismatches arising from differences in viewing geometry remains constrained by the computational cost of radiative-transfer modelling. We therefore developed a Bayesian neural network radiative-transfer emulator trained on the RTM Emulation Challenge dataset [1]. Radiative-transfer functions were compressed from 4,205 wavelength samples to 75 latent coefficients using fPCA before probabilistic spectral prediction. The emulator achieved over 1,500× acceleration relative to the reference workflow, with wavelength-resolved NRMSE values of 2-3% and predictive-interval coverage within 0.0145 of nominal confidence levels, indicating accurate spectral predictions and well-calibrated model uncertainty estimates when validated against independent MODTRAN simulations.

Even after observation-mismatch correction, residual radiometric differences may persist between sensors due to effects that are difficult to model explicitly. We therefore explored an optimal transport-based kernel regression as a data-driven correction approach. This method learns a mapping that aligns the statistical distributions of sensor and reference measurements, capturing discrepancies at the distribution level rather than fitting individual matchup residuals. Using Landsat-8 and RadCalNet matchups over the Gobabeb site, the approach demonstrated improved agreement between sensor and reference observations in an independent validation dataset.

Together, these methods demonstrate the potential of AI to complement physics-based cross-calibration through improved ROI selection, scalable uncertainty-aware observation mismatch correction, and data-driven modelling and correction of residual discrepancies.

b: The European Space Agency (ESA)-supported Generative Ground Control Point (GenCP) study investigates the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to produce geometrically consistent reference image chips from vector data for satellite image georeferencing and geometric calibration and validation (Cal/Val). Phase 1 demonstrated the feasibility of the concept using pix2pix-based paired image-to-image translation at two spatial scales: a 10 m Sentinel-2-based high-resolution (HR) configuration and a 50 cm very-high-resolution (VHR) configuration using imagery from several commercial satellite sensors [1,2]. The results showed that vector-derived synthetic imagery can support automated image matching, while also revealing limitations related to image– vector alignment, scene variability, sensor characteristics, seasonality, and training-data preparation.

GenCP Phase 2 advances the approach toward greater automation, generalization, and robustness across different imaging and geographic conditions. For VHR applications, pix2pixHD [3] was introduced and evaluated to improve the representation of fine spatial detail and complex urban structures. In parallel, preparation of vector-derived inputs was substantially automated: OpenStreetMap (OSM) data are converted directly into raster training masks, and the associated symbology has been enhanced to provide a richer and more consistent representation of semantic object classes. The VHR training and test database has also been expanded with additional imagery, including Pléiades, Pléiades Neo, SkySat, and Vantor WorldView-3 data, and with new test sites including Grosseto, Turin, La Crau, and Toulouse. Data from the different sensors are combined within the training dataset, enabling the robustness and generalization of a common generative model to be assessed under a broader range of scene and acquisition conditions.

A further development in the VHR workflow is the introduction of geographic coordinates as an additional conditioning input to pix2pixHD. Combined with the vector-derived masks, location information allows the model to learn geographically dependent radiometric and object-appearance characteristics while preserving the geometry encoded by the vector data. The generated imagery can therefore reflect regional differences in urban form and surface appearance, including variations in roof types, construction materials, vegetation, and overall radiometry between locations such as Ankara, Turin, Munich, and La Crau. This extends the framework from generic vector-to-image translation toward site-aware generation of reference imagery.

The HR branch has also been extended using a substantially larger training dataset while retaining the pix2pix framework. Two additional sources of information were investigated. First, Copernicus Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data were introduced as model input to assess whether topographic context improves the representation of terrain-related variability. Second, seasonality was explicitly incorporated through winter and summer imagery, enabling the model to account for seasonal changes in vegetation and surface appearance that cannot be represented by static vector masks alone.

The presentation will summarize the transition from the Phase 1 proof of concept to these Phase 2 developments, with emphasis on automated OSM processing, enhanced semantic representation, pix2pixHD-based VHR generation, coordinate-conditioned site awareness, DEM-supported HR modelling, seasonal training, and broader evaluation across sensors and test sites. Together, these developments aim to improve the scalability and operational readiness of GenCP for geometric Cal/Val and georeferencing applications within the ESA Earth observation context.

b: This research addresses spatial coregistration in 2D snapshot hyperspectral imagery captured by a tunable FPI. Along its orbit, Kuva Space’s Hyperfield-1 satellites acquire narrow spectral bands sequentially. Due to its high orbital velocity, successive acquisitions exhibit non-rigid geometric shifts. This spatial displacement degrades per-pixel spectral fidelity and, ultimately, complicates downstream parameter estimation.

A three-phase evaluation framework was developed, spanning spatial preprocessing analysis, alignment accuracy benchmarking, and hardware optimization. Different architectures were tested across a dataset provided by Kuva Space, consisting of 31 hyperspectral data cubes acquired by the Hyperfield-1A and Hyperfield-1B satellites. The dataset is structured according to the dual-channel payload architecture of the satellites. Each acquisition covers the VIS-NIR spectral range having a wavelength interval of 475nm
900nm and captures 22 spectral bands, with 2 spatial frames per band.
The three-phase framework is described below.

Phase 1: Quantitative Benchmarking and Efficiency Analysis This phase establishes a rigorous benchmarking framework to evaluate image coregistration methods, leveraging synthetic GT derived from known homography-based transformations. It considers three core configurations:
Mild Geometric Distortion: Simulate stable orbital acquisitions.
Crop Scale 66%, Rotation (θ) [-15°, 15°], Scaling (s) [0.8, 1.2], Overlap threshold ≥ 70%
Severe Geometric Distortion: Replicates high-agility maneuvers or extreme off-nadir observations.
Crop Scale 66%, Rotation (θ) [-50°, 50°], Scaling (s) [0.5, 2.0], Overlap threshold ≥ 30%
Combination of a Moderate Geometric Distortion and a Severe Radiometric Degradation: Simulate atmospheric interference and sensor degradation.

Crop Scale 90%, Rotation (θ) [-30°, 30°], Scaling (s) [0.9, 2.0], Overlap threshold ≥ 50% Radiometric transformations include: contrast alteration, brightness shift, gamma power-law correction, additive gaussian noise, additive uniform noise, salt-and-pepper dropout.

The primary objective is to systematically evaluate a spectrum of state-of-the-art architectures, to identify which models are most robust against high degrees of spatial and spectral distortion, while still retaining high alignment accuracy.
These models are grouped into three paradigms:
Detector-Based Methods: This workflow evaluates two primary architectures: ALIKED [1] paired with LightGlue [2], and SuperPoint [3] paired with SuperGlue [4].

Detector-Free Semi-Dense and Dense Matchers: The evaluated architectures in this category include LoFTR [5], its optimized derivative EfficientLoFTR [6], and the Robust Matching (RoMa) family (RoMa [7] and RoMaV2 [8]).
Multimodal Models and Foundation Paradigms: The pipeline integrates paradigms explicitly optimized for cross-spectral fusion such as XoFTR [9], MINIMA [10] and MatchAnything [11].

The benchmark data consists of misaligned image pairs, generated by sampling and applying a synthetic (ground truth) homography (HGT) transformation to one image. For each generated image pair, HGT is retained to later compare against the obtained alignment homography, to estimate the model performance..Performance is measured via the Area Under the Curve of reprojection error at strict (sub-)pixel thresholds (0.5𝑝𝑥, 1.0𝑝𝑥, 3.0𝑝𝑥, and 5.0𝑝𝑥).

Phase 2: Analysis of Feature Sparsity Mitigation To improve the robustness of the detection and matching of keypoints across multi-modal imagery, an analysis of pre-processing methods was performed. Failure modes were identified, such as low local contrast, high-frequency sensor noise, and extreme radiometric inversion, prior to feature extraction.

Phase 3: Hardware Optimization for High-Throughput Deployment The massive computational footprints of Deep Learning Models frequently trigger severe VRAM bottlenecks and out-of-memory (OOM) errors during the processing of large orbital data cubes. To improve inference efficiency, the two selected algorithms, i.e. EfficientLoFTR and the sparse ALIKED+LightGlue pipeline, are converted from their native, resource-intensive frameworks into optimized deployment formats. The models are first converted into the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) format, enabling subsequent compilation into highly optimized NVIDIA TensorRT engines. Quantization techniques are then applied to explicitly target the memory demands of the complex attention mechanisms. Finally, a rigorous comparative analysis is conducted across these deployment formats.

Results demonstrate that traditional sparse methods suffer from catastrophic keypoint starvation under extreme distortion. Conversely, incorporating universal foundation features, obtained using MatchAnything pretraining weights, successfully neutralized the modality gap.

The RoMA architecture initialized with MatchAnything pretraining weights established the absolute precision ceiling under radiometric and geometric stress, using the AUC at a strict 0.5-pixel matching threshold as the primary metric. However, its massive VRAM footprint and execution latency remain prohibitive for strict, real-time edge processing.

For spaceborne deployment, EfficientLoFTR initialized with MatchAnything weights and compiled into a TensorRT half-precision (FP16) engine emerged as the optimal operational compromise. It bypassed out-of-memory collapses, flattened VRAM allocation overhead, and reduced active forward-pass latency to 0.072 seconds while preserving robust sub-pixel localization accuracy.

Furthermore, preprocessing fine-tuning demonstrated that dense registration networks require model-specific spatial adjustments. RoMa variants maximized subpixel precision when integrated with a noise-suppressing Bilateral-CLAHE filter, whereas EfficientLoFTR required high-frequency statistical stabilization through a Wallis filter or a Fine-biased Multi-Scale CLAHE pipeline.

b: Full width at half maximum (FWHM) of a line/point spread function (LSF/PSF) is widely used as a key measure of spatial resolution in optical satellite imaging systems. Conventional FWHM estimation for high resolution 6 m or less satellite imagery typically relies on ground calibration and validation (Cal/Val) sites and line spread function analysis of sharp edge targets. Although accurate, this approach is constrained by the availability of suitable edge features, cloud free acquisitions, and enough pixels to construct a stable edge spread function. This study presents a image-similarity based semi-Monte Carlo technique for estimating FWHM from overlapping fifine resolution reference and target imagery. The method generates a series of target like images from a fifine resolution reference image by aggregating the reference data using difffferent weighting kernels and assumed FWHM values. The cross-correlation value (CCV) is calculated between each simulated image and the target image, and the FWHM corresponding to the maximum CCV is selected as the estimate. Simulation experiments using a 3 units target grid and FWHMs ranging from 3 units to 19 units demonstrated retrieval errors generally within 1 unit. The method was further evaluated using 119 real satellite target images in the red band over the Cal/Val sites, with fifine resolution WorldView-3 imagery serving as the reference. The results were compared with FWHM estimates derived from conventional Cal/Val site measurements. Overall, the proposed method produced results consistent with the Cal/Val based estimates, although performance degraded for some images because of image noise, temporal land cover changes, and difffferences between the aggregation kernel and the target sensor's system point spread function. The aggregation kernel of tent weighting provided improved performance over the equal weighting aggregation while offffering a computationally effiffifficient approximation to Gaussian-like weighting system responses. The use of a spectrally matched red-band reference image also produced more accurate FWHM estimates than a panchromatic reference image, demonstrating the importance of spectral consistency between the reference and target imagery. These results demonstrate that image-similarity based FWHM estimation can provide a practical alternative for spatial resolution assessment when dedicated Cal/Val edge targets are unavailable, while extending FWHM assessment to locations where suitable overlapping fifine resolution reference imagery is available.

b: Developed as part of the European Space Agency's DPR (Data Processors Re-engineering) project, ASGARD [1] is an open-source library dedicated to viewing geometry and sensor modeling. ASGARD, which rely on CSGROUP open-source library RUGGED [2] is used for geometric operations (localization, frame transformation, time processing, …) in Sentinel-1, 2, and 3 processing pipelines. ASGARD standardizes geometric operations, ensuring long-term maintainability, high portability, and the scalability required to support operational Sentinel missions.

Here, we present the recent developments led by CS GROUP to handle VHR push-broom sensor geometries, specifically targeting satellites like Pléiades. This work showcases ASGARD's flexibility as a generic modeling tool, proving its ability to support not only institutional Sentinel missions but also broader LEO VHR missions.

Very High Resolution (VHR) missions inherently necessitate highly precise and robust geometric refining. Within this framework, the specialized geometric refining library MORBIER (MOdel Refining By Iterative Estimation of Residue) has been successfully adapted to this context. This adaptation specifically enables the advanced management and processing of both Ground Control Points (GCPs) and tie points, thereby guaranteeing optimal mono and multi-view geometric consistency. Achieving this level of precision is critical to secure the rigorous geometric quality and performance required for downstream orthorectification and stereo-reconstruction workflows.

We will present the geometric quality results obtained from Pleiades tri-stereo triplets. The evaluation assesses the absolute and relative geometric performance, and consistency of the refinement pipeline. Thanks to the multi-view capability, we demonstrate a significant reduction in geometric bias, ensuring accuracy in both planimetry and altimetry.

b: Information on the plastic-mulched farmland (PMF) spatial distribution is essential for supporting precision agriculture and assessing its impact on climate and environment. However, accurate mapping of PMF remains challenging due to its small size relative to satellite data, variable shapes, seasonal dynamics, and short lifespan of visible PMF. In this paper, we present a method called Spatially Aware - Classifying Raw Irregular Time series (SA-CRIT) which maximizes the use of both temporal and spatial information for 2.5-m PMF mapping from Sentinel-2 time series without compositing. The approach extends the single-pixel, Transformer-based CRIT model to incorporate spatial patch modeling for patch-based irregular time series classification and integrates 10-m to 2.5-m super-resolution (SR) reconstruction to better address the challenges posed by small field sizes. The approach was applied to a globally representative PMF dataset across seven selected sites with label data generated using Sentinel-2 time series with the aid of high-resolution PlanetScope imagery. SA-CRIT can achieve an overall accuracy (OA) of 92.16% and a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 78.95% for 2.5-m resolution classifications across the seven study sites, outperforming its baseline CRIT model by 3.01% in OA and 4.23% in mIoU. Compared to the results from SA-CRIT when applied to 10-m Sentinel-2 time series, the 2.5-m SA-CRIT enhanced OA and mIoU by 1.40% and 2.73% respectively. In boundary regions, the 2.5-m results further improved OA by 4.12% and mIoU by 4.95%, demonstrating the effectiveness of SR for improving PMF classification results. A comprehensive spatial transferability assessment of SA-CRIT demonstrates its strong cross-regional adaptability

b: The global Earth observation (EO) landscape is evolving rapidly with the emergence of numerous public and commercial satellite missions offering unprecedented spatial, spectral, and temporal coverage. While this growth is expanding opportunities for innovation and operational applications, it also presents significant challenges in ensuring that data from diverse sources are comparable, interoperable, and scientifically trustworthy. Achieving these outcomes depends on robust calibration and validation (Cal/Val) practices that provide confidence in the physical integrity and consistency of satellite-derived products.

The Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) Working Group on Calibration and Validation (WGCV) plays a leading role in advancing international Cal/Val coordination by promoting harmonised methodologies, reference standards, inter-comparison activities, and community best practices. As the EO ecosystem becomes increasingly diverse, WGCV is broadening its focus beyond traditional government missions to facilitate greater engagement with commercial providers and emerging space organisations. This includes initiatives that leverage the well-established calibration heritage of public-sector missions to improve the quality, traceability, and interoperability of data from newer satellite systems.

This presentation reviews recent progress across WGCV activities that support cross-mission consistency, including developments in reference measurement networks, validation methodologies, quality assessment frameworks, and interoperability initiatives spanning both optical and radar observations. It also highlights collaborative efforts undertaken with other CEOS Working Groups, Virtual Constellations, and international partners to address common challenges associated with multi-sensor data integration and long-term Earth observation records.

The presentation underscores the growing role of community forums such as the Very High-Resolution Radar and Optical Data Assessment (VH-RODA) Workshop in bringing together government agencies, industry, and researchers to exchange knowledge, identify emerging challenges, and shape future Cal/Val priorities. These collaborative activities are helping establish the technical foundations needed to support reliable, harmonised EO products for scientific, environmental, and commercial applications.

b: Since its launch in April 2022, the German Earth observation satellite mission EnMAP has been delivering high-quality hyperspectral data to an expanding user community. The mission’s primary objective is to provide high-quality hyperspectral data for scientific research for a variety of applications, including vegetation and ecosystem monitoring, agriculture, inland and coastal water quality assessment, geological mapping, and soil characterization. Over the years, continuous updates have been implemented within the Ground Segment like new tasking strategies, processing chain updates, and enhanced calibration strategies. These improvements have increased data availability and system performance, as well as enabling emerging applications with EnMAP such as night-time light detection.

This presentation provides a comprehensive update regarding EnMAP’s operational status, focusing on the latest in-orbit calibration and instrument performance across radiometric, geometric, and spectral domains. We present recent assessments of instrument and calibration source stability, data quality, lunar observations, which are now conducted on a regular basis. All these efforts ensure the high quality and consistency of EnMAP’s Level-1 and Level-2 data products.

We also provide an overview of key developments in the data processing chain throughout the operational period, emphasizing the CEOS Analysis Ready Data (ARD) compliant L2A land product. Lessons learned from routine processing are shared, highlighting their implications for next-generation mission design, including ESA’s future CHIME mission.
Finally, brief examples of the consistency of EnMAP datasets are given, underpinning the benefits of a well-calibrated imaging spectrometer for other multi- and hyperspectral missions.

b: Recent advances in Artifificial Intelligence (AI) have increased the demand for executing detection, classifification, recognition and identifification algorithms on satellite imagery onboard to provide real- or near-real-time insights expanding beyond traditional RGB and multispectral sensors to also support hyperspectral imagers.

However, generating AI-ready onboard satellite imagery presents two key challenges: fifirst, adapting the image processing chain to the resource constraints, including limited computing power, memory, storage, energy and bandwidth; and second, processing the hyperspectral data, which comprise numerous narrow, contiguous spectral bands.

We present the onboard processing framework deployed by Loft on its YAM-6 satellite. This framework introduces two main innovations. First, it enables imagery acquired by the Dragonflfly Chameleon hyperspectral imager to be processed onboard leveraging Deimos Insight4EO’s image processing integration within Dragonflfly payloads, producing low latency, AI-ready data for onboard AI applications. Second, it provides an edge computing platform that supports the deployment of both Loft’s own AI applications and those developed by third-party customers. Together, these novel onboard capabilities enable low latency insights and reactive tip and cue operations via inter-satellite links (ISLs).

b: Mapping inundated areas after extreme storm events is particularly challenging in low-lying coastal wetlands due to complex land cover conditions, rapid environmental changes, and limited availability of cloud-free optical imagery. In this context, this study investigates the potential of combining Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), Sentinel-2 optical imagery, and machine learning (ML) techniques for flflood mapping in the Ebro Delta (Spain) during the Gloria storm event in January 2020. The analysis focuses on the classifification of flflooded and non-flflooded areas across heterogeneous aquatic and terrestrial environments using SAR amplitude, SAR coherence, and RGB optical features. Several ML algorithms, including Random Forest, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbours, and Multi-Layer Perceptron, were evaluated to determine the most effffective combination of input attributes and classifification approach. The results indicate that SAR-based features, particularly radar amplitudes and coherence, provide the highest classifification performance under severe storm conditions, whereas the inclusion of RGB optical data generally reduced classifification accuracy due to temporal inconsistencies and limitations associated with optical acquisitions during extreme weather events. The study highlights the robustness of SAR imagery for flflood mapping in complex coastal wetlands and confifirms the usefulness of ML-based approaches for analyzing inundation dynamics under adverse meteorological conditions.

b: Very-high-resolution optical image time series offffer increasing potential for urban-scale monitoring of building materials, but their operational use depends on reliable interpretation across changing acquisition conditions, sensor/viewing geometry and complex built environments. This poster presents an application-level validation case study for roof-level detection and change monitoring of probable asbestos-cement roofifing using very-high-resolution aerial optical imagery across Australian urban areas.

The study addresses data-quality challenges relevant to very-high-resolution Earth Observation products, including geometric misregistration, illumination variation, shadowing, obstruction and spectral similarity between roofifing materials. Roof objects were represented as image-patch sequences across seven temporal observations. A hybrid object-based deep learning framework was applied, combining DenseNet121 for spatial feature extraction with either LSTM or one-dimensional convolution for temporal modelling. Following binary roof-material classifification, post-classifification sequence alignment was used as a quality-control step to reduce temporal label inconsistency and improve roof-level change interpretation.

The framework achieved average overall accuracies of 95.8% and 96.0% for the DenseNet-LSTM and DenseNet-Conv1D models, respectively, with up to 94% asbestos-class detection accuracy on an independent test area. The resulting temporal outputs identify roof persistence, removal and change patterns.

The poster contributes to VH-RODA by showing how object-based roof representation, spatial–temporal deep learning and sequence alignment can improve the reliability of very-high-resolution optical image time series affffected by temporal inconsistency. It highlights a fifit-for-purpose AI workflflow for trustworthy roof-level change monitoring in urban environments.

b: As Earth observation capabilities continue to expand, there remains a critical need for well-characterized, coincident, ground-truthed datasets to validate algorithms and evaluate sensor performance. To address this need, the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) launched the RIT Open Community eXperiment (ROCX), a community-driven fifield campaign designed to bring together data providers, experimenters, and end users within an open-science framework.

ROCX 2025 was conducted over two weeks in September 2025 at the RIT Tait Preserve near Rochester, New York, USA. More than 75 researchers representing 24 organizations from six countries participated in the campaign. Nineteen coordinated fifield experiments were conducted to address a diverse range of remote sensing challenges, while 31 unique sensing platforms collected more than 18 TB of data. Data acquisitions included six satellite providers, two crewed aerial platforms, eight unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and multiple ground-based instruments. These assets captured a broad range of sensing modalities, including multispectral, hyperspectral, thermal infrared, polarized, lidar, and high-resolution RGB basemap imagery, providing a rich, multi-scale dataset for calibration, validation, and algorithm development activities.

A key objective of ROCX is the creation and dissemination of openly accessible reference datasets. ROCX 2025 products are currently being compiled and distributed through an open-access data portal that includes curated remote sensing collections, ground-truth measurements, and investigator-provided experiment packages. By providing community access to both imagery and supporting validation data, ROCX aims to accelerate research, promote reproducibility, and enable benchmarking across diverse Earth observation applications.

The strong participation and broad international interest in ROCX 2025 demonstrate a signifificant demand for coordinated open-data fifield campaigns. Building on this momentum, planning is underway for ROCX 2027. This presentation will provide an overview of ROCX 2025 accomplishments, the evolving open-access data archive, and opportunities for participation in ROCX 2027.

b: The new IRIDE programme is the Italian Earth Observation (EO) "constellation of constellations" system, coordinated by the European Space Agency (ESA) with the support of the Italian Space Agency (ASI) [1, 2]. It is deploying several high-resolution optical constellations, including OHB Italia's Eaglet-2 and Argotec's Hawk for Earth Observation (HEO) [2, 3]. For these data to be used reliably in downstream services and Analysis Ready Data (ARD) workflows, every product must carry a consistent per-pixel assessment of cloud and cloud-shadow contamination. Small-satellite optical sensors, however, typically lack the dedicated spectral channels (such as cirrus or thermal bands) used by conventional cloud-detection algorithms. Training mission-specific models would also require large-labelled datasets that do not yet exist for newly launched constellations.

Here we present an operational IRIDE cloud-masking processor that applies OmniCloudMask (OCM) [4], a sensor-agnostic deep-learning model for cloud and cloud-shadow segmentation, to Eaglet-2 and HEO imagery without mission-specific retraining. The processor ingests Level-1C (L1C) products, converts digital numbers to top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance using calibration coefficients from the product metadata, extracts the valid-data footprint, resamples the imagery to the model's inference resolution, and performs full-scene segmentation. It produces an enriched L1C product containing the original imagery and three additional outputs: a cloud mask retaining the full OCM class scheme (clear, thick cloud, thin cloud, cloud shadow, and no data); a per-pixel cloud-confidence map derived from the model predictions; and SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)-compliant metadata reporting scene-level cloud cover and per-class statistics.

The processor is built for integration into the IRIDE Payload Data Ground Segment (PDGS). It complies with the IRIDE Processor Interface Control Document (ICD), runs in data-driven mode unattended in a containerized and fully offline environment on central or graphics processing units (CPU/GPU), and produces deterministic, reproducible results. In this work we will detail the processing chain and results over a range of Eaglet-2 and HEO acquisitions. We will assess how well OCM's predictions transfer to these sensors across different surface types and cloud conditions, using independent reference masks. We will also discuss the strengths and limitations of applying a pre-trained, sensor-agnostic model to new commercial constellations, particularly for thin clouds, bright surfaces and cloud shadows, and consider how per-pixel confidence information can support cloud-mask quality indicators in commercial EO products.

b: It is widely recognised that measurement uncertainty and error-covariance information is an essential part of Earth Observation (EO) products. Users need sufficient information to determine whether a dataset is fit for purpose and to propagate its uncertainty through subsequent analysis. However, in practice, uncertainty information is represented inconsistently across EO and environmental datasets. If provided at all, different terminology and structures are used, while important information may be recorded only in documentation or omitted entirely.

To address this problem, the Uncertainty metadata Naming Convention (UNC) has been developed. A human- and machine-readable approach for recording uncertainty information alongside observational and model data. UNC defines standard attributes to describe how measurement variables are associated with individual uncertainty components and how their units, probability distributions and error-correlation properties are described. Importantly, error-correlation can be represented in compact parameterisations across spatial, temporal, spectral and other dimensions, avoiding the need to store impractically large error-covariance matrices. It is already implemented for the Hypernets network, and under consideration for future mission products, such as the Copernicus expansion CHIME sensor.

In recent months, UNC has undergone a community beta phase and has been proposed for inclusion in the widely adopted Climate and Forecast (CF) Conventions. This represents an important step towards establishing UNC as standard framework for uncertainty representation of environmental data. This poster presentation will describe the standard and present examples from its application to selected datasets.

b: DIVA (Demonstration of an Integrated approach for the Validation and exploitation of Atmospheric missions) is a python jupyter notebook-based platform aiming to collect, handle, and exploit atmospheric data from satellite, ground-based remote sensing instruments, in-situ and modelling products and to build new synergies and validation approaches beyond the operational products.

Previously, DIVA had demonstrated the capability and versatility of such a system to integrate ground-based (lidar, ceilometer, sun/lunar photometer, and spectrometer), satellite and model data, stand-alone, and synergetic algorithms for advanced data products, using combined algorithms from difffferent platforms and sensors, as well as innovative data mining and data visualization tools.

The new DIVA platform and project is used as a centralised hub for EarthCARE Calibration and Validation activities, focusing on aerosol and cloud products. The platform ensures adequate data access and user management of the dedicated cal/val teams to EarthCARE L1 and L2 products as well as to ground-based measurements through EVDC.

Moreover, in DIVA users do have the possibility for science exploration and exploitation of ground based and satellite products by taking advantage of the GRASP (Generalized Retrieval of Atmosphere and Surface Properties) and NATALI (Neural network Aerosol Typing Algorithm based on LIdar data) algorithms to further exploit aerosol related products from ground-based datasets as well as ESA’s Atmosphere Virtual Lab. All these tools have been integrated in the DIVA platform for its users.

This contribution highlights DIVA as the centralized hub for EarthCARE Calibration and Validation activities, focusing on aerosol and cloud products. The platform is available for the dedicated working groups for both aerosol and cloud validation with adequate user and data management as well for other scientists developing new and/or improved lidar, radar, photometer, and spectrometer related products.

b: A fundamental function of an optical remote sensing sensor relies on its ability to discern ground objects in agreement with Earth Observation mission design specifications. In the community, this notion is addressed by using spatial resolution analysis technics.
From user perspective, analysis requires a good knowledge of Level 1 data quality metrics.

Taken benefits of knowledge and experience learnt with Image Quality analysis undertook within the framework of the EDAP / EDAP+ project [1], best practice documents [2], [3], [4], and also inter comparison exercise activities made with CEOS members [5], the idea of developing an open-source tool dedicated to image quality analysis merged.

The objective of this presentation is to showcase The Image Quality Toolset software solution [6]. Developed in the context of the ESA Artificial Intelligence for Quality Control (AI4QC project), this software proposes functionalities to estimate IQ related parameters as Modulation Transfer Function (MTF), Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM), Singal to Noise Ratio (SNR).

A key advantage of this product is its operational flexibility, as it can be used either through the graphical interface of Quantum Geographic Information System (QGIS) or via a command-line interface. It has been developed for remote sensing Calibration / Validation users as a supporting tool for Quality Control (QC) of satellite image.

The development of this tool required a substantial amount efforts spent in different and various areas. Also, it is proposed to discuss within this presentation the s/w architecture, functions external resources, the test dataset production (simulation), the proposed MTF and SNR algorithms and finally validation results will be shared.

A second advantage of this tool is to generate standardized MTF/SNR reports that can be shared across community and understood at a broader scale, Also, an another point into this presentation, is to describe QC report and content. The Image Quality Toolset was inspired by the QGIS MTF Tool [7], as our goal was to enable operators to assess product performance efficiently and consistently. Finaly, the concept has been extended; the tool estimates more parameters, compute more metrics, implement more methods (MTF Knife Edge, MTF Bridge, SNR JACIE, SNR FFT …) and propose user to select among a large diversity of models (edge models for instance).

b: The progressing radiometric and geometric potential of small EO satellites, opposing requirements from commercial and national operators, as well as increasing expectations from downstream applications, have put pressure on payload data ground systems (PDGS). Commercial PDGS are facing challenges to offer a more competitive and complete services package (from simulation and tasking, through cal/val, to processing and distribution), and to ensure repeatability on various missions without substantial internal redesigns. This progression naturally comes with maintaining the right cost balance.

In mid-2025, World from Space finished a prototype of the Orbis payload data system and onboarded a first operational mission, Saturnin-1, from VZLU Aerospace. Since then, it has successfully maintained this mission in the system, continually validating its performance and distributing data to the end users. We are currently developing an entirely new version of the system within an ESA framework project based on lessons learnt. The main goals are to increase data sovereignty by agnostic platform deployment (cloud and on premise), improve the support for pushbroom missions, solidify frameworks for systematic payload model handling and nominal processing, and design a calibration blueprint for timely cal/val routines for mission operators. In the poster, we describe the ongoing R&D activities behind these goals and further present other strategic projects focused on on-board data processing and EO supply chain veracity capacity-building. We also address the challenges of cooperating on the upcoming Czech multi-tenant optical mission AMBIC.

b: As part of the Copernicus Programme, the European Commission (EC) and the European Space Agency (ESA) are expanding the Copernicus Space Component and implementing satellite remote measurements for supporting anthropogenic CO₂ and CH₄ emission monitoring. In support of well-informed policy decisions and for assessing the effectiveness of strategies for CO₂ and methane, CH₄ emission reduction, uncertainties associated with current anthropogenic emission estimates at national and regional scales need to be reduced. Satellite measurements of atmospheric CO₂ and CH₄, complemented by in-situ measurements and bottom-up inventories, will be elaborated in an advanced (inverse) modelling scheme to provide a transparent and consistent quantitative assessment of their emissions and their trends at the scale of megacities, regions, countries, and at global scale.

Operational monitoring of anthropogenic emissions requires high precision CO₂ and CH₄ observations with, on average, weekly effective coverage at mid-latitudes and spatial resolution of 4 km2. The Copernicus Anthropogenic CO₂ Monitoring (CO2M) Mission will provide these observations from NIR and SWIR radiance spectra at a spectral resolution of 0.12 nm and 0.35 nm, respectively. The measurements will be complemented by (1) aerosol observations, to minimise light-path related biases, and (2) NO2 observations as tracer to emissions from high temperature combustion, and (3) cloud imaging to further facilitate the retrieval of CO₂ and CH₄ by identifying measurements contaminated by low clouds and high-altitude cirrus.

The CO2M mission will form a keystone in supporting international activities. The Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) and the Coordination Group for Meteorological Satellites (CGMS) recognize that high-quality, systematic observations of atmospheric CO₂ and CH₄ from space-based sensors can make critical contributions to an integrated global greenhouse gas (GHG) observing system. In the joint CEOS-CGMS Working Group on Climate (WGClimate), a dedicated GHG Task Team has developed and is implementing the “Roadmap for a coordinated implementation of carbon dioxide and methane monitoring from space”.

In this presentation, we will provide an overview of the CO2M mission with a focus on its greenhouse gas measurement capability. The presentation will further provide an overview of international coordination activities related to greenhouse gas observations from space. We will outline the approach for delivering fit-for-purpose products, to be co-developed with stakeholders providing actionable information for greenhouse gas monitoring policies and provide an overview of the engagement with stakeholders.

b: IRIDE is the Italian Earth Observation programme, consisting of multiple satellite missions with complementary sensing capabilities and a common ground segment infrastructure. This paper focuses on the HEO and Eaglet-2 optical missions, comprising 15 and 16 satellites currently in orbit respectively, and on the calibration and validation (Cal/Val) activities conducted to assess their in-orbit performance and related product quality.

The work presents the Cal/Val strategy developed for both missions and the main results achieved during commissioning and early operational phases. The adopted approach addresses geometric, radiometric, and image quality performance through the use of dedicated reference sites, independent reference datasets, and mission-specifific processing chains. Particular emphasis is placed on the quantifification of geometric, radiometric and image-quality performance, the identifification and characterisation of residual systematic effffects, and the long-term monitoring of product stability. Special attention is given to the standardisation and automation of Cal/Val processes across large satellite constellations, enabling a consistent assessment methodology and effiffifficient monitoring of multiple spacecraft and products throughout their operational lifetime.

Selected in-orbit results from HEO and Eaglet-2 are presented, highlighting absolute geometric accuracy, absolute radiometric performance, modulation transfer function (MTF), and overall image quality assessment. The analysis also describes the corrective actions and processing refifinements introduced during commissioning to address identifified anomalies and optimise product quality. Beyond the results achieved for the individual missions, the study demonstrates how a common Cal/Val framework can support the effiffifficient validation of large optical constellations, ensuring consistency, repeatability and scalability across an increasing number of sensors and satellites.

The experience gained from both missions provides valuable lessons learned and contributes to the defifinition of a harmonised, scalable, and mission-agnostic Cal/Val framework for current and future optical constellations. More broadly, the proposed approach aims at establishing some guidelines that can support the calibration and validation of forthcoming national and international Earth observation missions.

b: Satellite and reanalysis products are increasingly used in operational water management. However, their quality flags are designed for global consistency, while the conditions that affect accuracy differ by region. In this study, region-specific quality control criteria were developed for ASCAT soil moisture, GPM IMERG precipitation, MOD16A2 evapotranspiration, and ERA5-Land snow depth over the Korean Peninsula, 2018-2025. For soil moisture, observations were screened for frozen ground, snow cover, complex topography, and failed retrievals. The ASCAT frozen and snow probability fields are long-term climatological values rather than conditions on the day of observation; freeze and snow screening instead used ERA5-Land soil temperature and snow depth matched to each observation. For precipitation, the quality index of each half-hourly field was used; for evapotranspiration, the cloud and algorithm bits of the quality layer. ERA5-Land provides no quality flags; physical range checks and comparison with IMS snow cover were used instead. Each threshold was set from the physical basis stated in the product documentation together with its measured accuracy against in situ observations. Anomaly-based, standardized-anomaly and quantile-mapping bias corrections were then applied to the screened data and evaluated with continuous and detection metrics. The best-performing method for each variable was extended over the grid by interpolating station statistics. Across all four products, the observations removed by screening agreed less closely with in situ measurements than those retained, indicating that the criteria identified poor-quality data rather than reducing coverage. Bias correction improved correlation and reduced bias for all variables. This approach provides a basis for developing national guidelines for the quality management of Earth observation data.

b: This study presents the atmospheric assessment performed within the Earth Data Assessment Platform (EDAP+) on two innovative commercial Earth Observation products: the GHGSat Level-4 (L4) CO₂ emission-rate dataset and the SPIRE GNSS Polarimetric Radio Occultation (PRO) products. The objective is to evaluate products quality and scientific consistency.

For the GHGSat CO₂ product, a validation exercise was conducted using 236 acquisitions over power plants located in the United States and Europe. Reference emissions were derived from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Clean Air Markets Program dataset and, for European sites, from plant energy-generation records converted into CO₂ emission rates through tailored coefficients. GHGSat retrievals slightly underestimated reference values in approximately 72% of cases, likely reflecting the snapshot of satellite observations compared with hourly plant-wide inventories. Wind speed was identified as a contributing factor to retrieval discrepancies, highlighting the need for further optimization of detection thresholds and algorithms, particularly over Europe. The overall analysis indicates a fair agreement between the GHGSat CO2 emissions rate, and the reference data. The assessment nevertheless confirms the potential of GHGSat’s high-resolution CO₂ monitoring capability, which provides facility-scale emission attribution from space (Credits to GHGSat support).

The next decade is expected to witness the development of complementary CO₂ monitoring architectures, combining high-resolution commercial systems capable of facility-scale plume attribution, such as GHGSat and Carbon Mapper, with operational public missions such as CO2M and MicroCarb, designed to provide systematic monitoring of anthropogenic emissions from industrial clusters, urban areas and national territories. Together, these missions will substantially enhance the global capability to independently quantify and verify CO₂ emissions from space.

The SPIRE PRO analysis focused on the capability of polarimetric GNSS radio occultation measurements to detect precipitation signatures through differential phase delay. Comparisons with GPM IMERG precipitation products and between different SPIRE processing levels showed that excess-phase observables are sensitive to hydrometeor presence, consistent with recent literature and independent evaluations of the Spire PRO mission. The analysis highlighted the scientific value of high-frequency (50 Hz) phase measurements. Recent studies further demonstrate that Spire’s PRO constellation provides thousands of observations per day and exhibits sensitivity to precipitation intensity and vertical hydrometeor structure, supporting future meteorological applications (Credits to SPIRE support).

Recent demonstrations from Spire and precursor RHO-PAZ missions indicate that the polarimetric observables are sensitive to hydrometeor content, opening the possibility for future assimilation of precipitation-related information once appropriate forward models, error characterization and validation activities are established.

b: Absolute Geolocation Accuracy (ABS) monitoring is critical for maintaining product quality, resolving customer issues, and meeting strict geometric specififications (e.g., CE90 < 5 m) across satellite flfleets. With the continuous expansion of Planet's flfleet, the demand for scalable, automated quality pipelines operating in near real-time grows alongside it. However, evaluating satellite products against Independent Reference (IR) imagery introduces unquantifified uncertainty, as reference datasets themselves are rarely validated against ground truth. This study addresses this gap by establishing a methodology for validated "golden test sites", reference locations where systematic geodetic offffsets and imagery distortions are quantifified and corrected using Ground Control Points (GCPs). Thereby ensuring an unbiased baseline for automated flfleet monitoring.
Using Planet's SuperDove constellation as a primary case study , 119 surveyed GCPs across ten global test sites were matched to high-resolution aerial reference imagery to derive

horizontal errors, root mean square error (RMSE), 90% circular error (CE90), and displacement vectors. Across all evaluated sites, the overall positional accuracy was 1.37 m RMSE and 2.08 m CE90, revealing clear regional variations in both the magnitude and direction of displacement. When evaluated against the ASPRS standard requiring reference data to be at least three times more accurate than the evaluated sensor, three sites fail to meet the required threshold.

Systematic offffsets arise from both geodetic effffects and intrinsic uncertainties in the underlying aerial imagery. Unmodelled tectonic drift and epoch discrepancies, compounded by outdated GCP survey dates, manifest as positional biases because of how WGS 84 coordinates drift over time relative to static, plate-fifixed IR datums. These discrepancies are most pronounced at sites with datum inconsistencies or lower-accuracy reference imagery, particularly in the United States where CE95 is approximately 4 m, whereas sites tied to plate-fifixed datums on the Eurasian and African plates exhibit consistently sub-metre offffsets.

Overall, while Planet's IR datasets demonstrate strong internal geometric consistency, their suitability as an absolute reference is constrained by tectonic drift, outdated survey epochs, and source imagery limitations. To resolve these limitations, establishing GCP-validated "golden testsites" requires harmonising GCP coordinates to a common epoch and correcting systematic IR offffsets. Implementing these validated test sites provides an immediate solution to eliminate reference bias in SuperDove evaluations, supporting the long-term vision of using exclusively calibrated golden sites for operational ABS evaluations across Planet’s expanding satellite flfleets.

b: Calibration and Validation activities rely on a large and heterogeneous body of technical information, spread across scientific reports, product documentation and validation material. A key challenge lies in the multimodal nature of this information: critical results are often contained not only in text, but also in tables, plots, figures and images. Efficiently extracting, connecting and retrieving information across these different modalities is therefore essential to properly exploit Cal/Val knowledge.

To address this challenge, we present an AI-powered assistant designed to facilitate access to Cal/Val information through a conversational interface. The system combines Large Language Models with Retrieval-Augmented Generation techniques to retrieve and synthesize information from heterogeneous and multimodal Cal/Val resources while maintaining traceability to the underlying sources.

The proposed pipeline places particular emphasis on multimodal data ingestion, with the objective of preserving and making searchable the information contained in textual and visual elements. This knowledge base is then exploited through a hybrid retrieval and inference pipeline to provide contextualized answers to user queries.

Beyond a conventional RAG pipeline, the current work investigates an agentic reasoning loop allowing the system to iteratively analyse a request, retrieve additional information when necessary, and combine information across multiple sources and modalities.

A dedicated evaluation framework is used to benchmark successive versions of the pipeline and identify limitations in information extraction, retrieval and answer generation. Current work focuses on consolidating the prototype and improving its ability to exploit complex multimodal Cal/Val documentation.
This work investigates how recent advances in multimodal AI, LLMs, RAG and agentic approaches can support Cal/Val experts in navigating and exploiting technical knowledge.
Rather than replacing expert analysis, the proposed assistant aims to make information distributed across complex Cal/Val resources more directly accessible and usable.
This work is sponsored by the European Space Agency (ESA).

b: Earth Observation (EO) data and EO value-added products, such as land cover maps, vegetation indices, and flood maps, are traditionally highly reliable sources of information. However, they are increasingly vulnerable to sophisticated alterations and cyber threats. In an era marked by the rise of fake news and AI-generated content, ensuring the veracity of both EO datasets and their derived products has become critical. Falsified or tampered EO data can distort reality and rapidly spread misinformation, undermining the credibility of data-driven decisions across many fields, such as climate research, disaster response and defence monitoring.
Led by Telespazio UK and supported by security experts FACTiven and Leonardo, as well as EO data chain experts, the ESA EO Veracity Proof of Concept Verification project addresses this challenge by:
Identifying vulnerabilities in the EO end-to-end information generation chain.
Characterising potential interference types and their consequences.
Proposing countermeasures and methodologies for their integration.

The team will present the EO Veracity project and summarise the potential vulnerabilities of an EO end-to-end information generation chain identified during the first phase of the project. To find out more about the project visit https://eoveracity.ssl.telespazio.com/.

b: NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA) Program is a science-enabling program that provides licensed access to high‑quality commercial Earth observation data. The program enhances data reliability through calibration and validation partnerships, transparent evaluation processes, and funding for new science and application use cases that help transform commercial datasets into actionable research and applied solutions.

The program augments NASA’s gold standard fleet of freely and openly available Earth observing satellite observations and data products with high-resolution, high-frequency, and taskable commercial datasets.

This presentation will share an update on the CSDA program’s work and accomplishments since VH RODA 2025. b: The Copernicus Land Surface Temperature Monitoring (LSTM) mission and the CNES/ISRO TRISHNA mission will, for the fifirst time, deliver thermal infrared observations at 50–60 m with a revisit of a few days, making the thermal regime of rivers and small lakes observable from space. To prepare for the Calibration and Validation of these observations, reference measurements are needed. Spaceborne radiometers sense the skin layer, whereas current in-situ river networks measure bulk temperature at depth which is not directly comparable and cannot be converted directly to skin temperature. The CEOS LPV protocol for land surface temperature validation requires surface-leaving radiance, minute-scale sampling, matchups within ~30 minutes of overpass and homogeneous targets: requirements that hydrology-oriented networks, designed for flflood monitoring and hourly to daily sampling, do not meet. The consequence is documented — Landsat retrievals degrade from ~1.4 °C RMSE on a 250 m-wide reach to ~4.7 °C on a 50 m-wide one, mixed water/bank pixels dominating the error budget at the very scales LSTM and TRISHNA will resolve.

vorteX-io addresses this gap with the micro-station: a compact, non-contact in-situ instrument derived from satellite altimetry, installed in hours on any bridge or riverbank without civil works. A single device delivers in real time a complete hydro-meteorological suite — water surface height, discharge, velocity, water surface temperature, rainfall, and calibrated images of the reach — with onboard AI processing at the edge and cloud delivery within seconds. Installed several meters above the water and measuring remotely, it is immune to flflood damage and drift, and can be densifified at a cost per monitored kilometer far below conventional instrumentation. For thermal Cal/Val, the micro-station observes water surface temperature using infrared thermal sensor, in the same skin layer sensed by the satellite, and applies a deep-learning water mask that isolates water pixels from banks, that isolates water from banks and confifirms that the sounded footprint contains water only. The onboard LiDAR used for water surface height flflags dry-bed conditions independently of the imagery, and remains available at night, so that thermal samples over an exposed bed never enter a matchup. The infrared thermal sensor integrates each measurement in a few seconds, so that water surface temperature is sampled at sub-minute rate. Each micro-station operates continuously and additionally synchronizes a dedicated acquisition with the exact moment of a satellite overpass, removing the temporal mismatch that can impact thermal matchup budgets, while the calibrated imagery documents the state of the reach and the representativeness of the footprint. Comparisons against immersed reference probes have been running since early 2023 on Adour-Garonne basins thanks to a network of 145 micro-stations deployed with the Adour-Garonne Water Agency, CNES and the French Offiffiffice for Biodiversity, with encouraging results.

We propose to transpose to the thermal domain the operational FRM provision model established by ESA for altimetry over inland waters. In St3TART and St3TART-FO, vorteX-io operates micro-stations at inland-water super-sites and delivers FRM in near-real-time within the ESA FRM chain for the operational Cal/Val activities of the Sentinel-3 altimetry mission (measuring water surface height) over inland waters. The same construction is possible for water surface temperature: dedicated FRM protocols and procedures, SI traceability of the radiometric chain with pre- and post-deployment characterization, a maintained uncertainty budget, documented quality control, and an explicit skin-to-bulk parametrization derived from paired radiometric and immersed references; a roadmap arbitrating permanent versus campaign FRM; and multi-variable, multi-mission super-sites co-located with existing altimetry super-sites, so that one site serves LSTM, TRISHNA, Sentinel-3 SLSTR, Landsat and the altimetry constellation at once. We propose to present this concept and to discuss with the LSTM and TRISHNA Cal/Val teams the requirements an operational thermal FRM service should meet.

b: constellr is developing a satellite-based Earth observation system designed to provide frequent, global land surface temperature (LST) observations for applications including ecological monitoring, resource management, and defence and intelligence.

Since early 2025, constellr has been deploying its fifirst-generation of SkyBee instruments within the HiVE constellation. They belong to to the 100 kg microsatellite class and carry a cryocooled four-band thermal infrared (TIR) camera and a visible/near-infrared (VNIR) camera covering similar spectral bands as those from Sentinel-2 below 1 µm. The VNIR measurements deliver contextual and complementary information along with the thermal data.

Achieving an LST accuracy of 2 K without dedicated onboard calibration devices requires a stringent combination of operational radiometric calibration, relative calibration between observations, geometric processing, and advanced algorithms for deriving surface temperature from the measured radiances.
This presentation provides an overview of the current HiVE constellation data quality and presents recent developments in the ground processing chain addressing three key aspects of the system.

First, we present the current status of the HiVE data quality, including assessments of radiometric accuracy, geometric accuracy, and image sharpness. These results provide an overview of the performance achieved with the currently operational satellites and identify the main contributors to residual uncertainties. Second, we present recent improvements in the LST retrieval algorithm. This new TESlib approach relies on a spectral emissivity library and exploits the spectral information contained in the measured radiances to better constrain surface emissivity, leading to more robust retrieved land surface temperatures.

Finally, we present a new processing approach for mitigating a signifificant spatial blurring effffect observed in the VNIR data acquired by the Simerasens cameras. Conventional PSF estimation and deconvolution approaches have proven inadequate due to the strongly non-Gaussian characteristics of the observed point-spread function. We therefore developed and trained a convolutional neural network for image sharpening and integrated this approach into the processing chain. Results demonstrate improvement in spatial image quality and illustrate the potential of learned restoration methods for addressing sensor-specifific imaging characteristics.

Together, these developments demonstrate the ongoing evolution of the HiVE calibration and processing chain and their contribution to improving the quality, reliability, and scientifific usability of HiVE-derived surface temperature and reflflectance products.

b: The increasing amount of geo-spatial data goes in-line with the increasing number of Earth observation satellites in space. The integration of this spaceborne data in large storage data cubes allows the analysis of continental to global phenomena with machine-learning techniques but requires consistent and accurate geolocation of the various input data. The unprocessed imagery contains distortions of various magnitudes depending on the off-nadir viewing angle but also on the local topography imaged by the sensor. The final geolocation accuracy depends on a detailed knowledge of the sensors’ viewing geometry but also the digital elevation data used on the ground segment processing chain (i.e. for the orthorectification process step).

The 30m and 90m instances of Copernicus DEM (GLO-30 & GLO-90) can be accessed via a free-and-open data policy from ESA and both represent a consistent and accurate Digital Surface Model (DSM) with input data acquired between December 2010 and January 2015. However, Earth surface is changing due to anthropogenous and environmental processes and relevant height data for the orthorectification process must be kept up-to-date but also upgraded in terms of resolution to keep pace with the improvement in spatial resolution of recent and future satellites.

This presented study will compare various orthorectification results of VHR Pléiades and Pléiades Neo satellite imagery in plain but also mountainous topographic terrain. In addition, a differentiation between urban and rural environments is applied when presenting the results of an absolute geolocation study and corresponding visual analysis. The DEM data used for orthorectification is the Copernicus DEM in its 30m version (CopDEM GLO-30; acquired 2010 to 2015) as well as more current Airbus 3D World data (5 meters; input data acquired since 2017 until at least February 2026). Both DEMs stem from the TanDEM-X mission. A major improvement is the rapid availability of an error-free DEM version after raw data acquisition which allows improved alignment of the EM used for orthorectification to the acquisition date of the satellite-based VHR imagery. A tailoring of Airbus 3D World DSM for orthorectification purposes is also presented.

b: The MELA-SUPFIX project (Multisource Earth observation integration for an improved assessment of LAnd processes), funded by ESA, aims to build an integrated remote sensing framework for field-scale monitoring of Water Use Efficiency (WUE) and Nitrogen Use Efficiency (NUE), exploiting synergies among Sentinel-2 and the upcoming FLEX, CHIME, LSTM and ROSE-L missions. Structured into a Preparatory Period, an Extended Observation Period and two Intensive Observation Periods (IOP1: 11-22 May, winter-cereal vegetation peak; IOP2: 20-31 July, irrigated summer-crop peak), the campaign combined coordinated ground, UAV and airborne acquisitions. b: As the demand for high-frequency, high-resolution Earth observation data grows, ensuring consistent image quality across a large and dynamic satellite constellation is essential. In order to maintain transparency, uphold rigorous data standards, and build user trust, we are introducing Satellogic's Periodical Image Quality Report. While we rely on a wide array of internal measurements for continuous payload monitoring, this new report is specifically designed to be public-facing and focuses on evaluating our data using standardized, commonly accepted methodologies across the Earth observation community.

This presentation outlines the operational methodologies we have developed to routinely assess and monitor key image quality metrics across our optical payloads. Specifically, we will detail our approaches for measuring and tracking the main spatial, geometric, and radiometric image quality metrics.

During the talk, we will provide a brief overview of the analytical methods and calibration techniques applied to extract these metrics. We will present examples of the results, demonstrating the current performance baseline of our sensors. We will also discuss the operational and technical difficulties we face in implementing and standardizing these measurements across a dynamic environment.

An important objective of this quality assessment framework is to be built for scale. We will emphasize our ongoing commitment to applying these automated methodologies to evaluate every single satellite in our expanding fleet. By doing so, we ensure that the entire constellation is systematically characterized and that our users can rely on consistent, quantified quality metrics for all acquired imagery.

b: HR satellite imagery is increasingly used as a basis for decision-making, sometimes with a major legal or human impact. This raises the question of whether such imagery can be trusted. In the frame of the Sentinel Optical Mission Performance Cluster (OPT-MPC), we have applied uncertainty analysis to Sentinel imagery and strived to generate representative per-pixel uncertainty. The methodology and principles are generally applicable to similar optical imagers. We will present the current status and open points for the uncertainty models.

b: Earth Observation (EO) products increasingly support critical decision-making in domains such as disaster response, environmental monitoring, climate research, and defence. As EO data passes through complex processing and dissemination chains, its veracity can be affected by intentional or unintentional interferences occurring at different stages, from data acquisition through processing to distribution. Ensuring confidence in an EO product therefore requires not only securing access to the underlying systems but also understanding how the data itself may be altered and how its integrity and authenticity can be verified throughout its lifecycle.

The ESA EO Veracity Proof of Concept Verification project has investigated these challenges through a systematic analysis of the end-to-end EO data supply chain. Building on the identification of EO assets and attack surfaces, the project has characterised potential interference scenarios and analysed technical countermeasures that can contribute to their mitigation.

This presentation will summarise the main results of this analysis, focusing on the vulnerabilities analysis across the EO end-to-end data chain for manipulation that could undermine trust in EO products and services. In addition, the presentation will discuss the assessment of suitable countermeasures including data integrity, authenticity mechanisms, provenance, and traceability.

Looking ahead, the presentation will explore the project's vision for establishing a scalable EO Veracity framework and methodology. The aim is to provide stakeholders with a structured approach for assessing veracity risks, implementing appropriate safeguards, and increasing confidence in EO data and value-added products. By creating a framework that can be applied across diverse EO processing chains, the project seeks to support the long-term trustworthiness and operational reliability of EO information in an increasingly complex threat environment.
To find out more about the project visit: https://eoveracity.ssl.telespazio.com/

b: GHGSat operates a constellation of high-resolution satellites purpose-built for imaging and quantifying methane point-source emissions, comprising 16 methane satellites in low Earth orbit. Satellite-based methane monitoring is increasingly used to support emissions reporting and mitigation, but its adoption in regulatory and voluntary frameworks depends on a rigorous, transparent characterization of system performance under real-world conditions. We present a comprehensive validation of the GHGSat constellation's detection and quantification performance based on a multi-campaign controlled-release dataset spanning 2021 to 2026, comprising 140 releases that combine GHGSat's self-organized campaigns with independent third-party experiments conducted by Stanford University, FluxLab, and TADI.

To characterize detection performance, we develop a probabilistic model in which the probability of detection depends on the plume signal-to-noise ratio, itself a function of emission rate, wind speed, retrieval noise, and spatial resolution. This conditions-dependent formulation, benchmarked using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria against several model variants, yields a 50% probability of detection of 99.0 ± 5.3 kg/h under median controlled-release conditions (3 m/s wind speed, 7 mmol/m² column noise, 27 m resolution). This estimate converges stably as the dataset grows and remains consistent when independent single-blind samples are added to the self-organized releases, supporting the robustness of the approach.

Quantification accuracy is assessed through parity analysis of estimated versus metered emission rates, yielding a linear regression slope of 0.93 ± 0.03 (R² = 0.92) using operationally available wind products, improving to 0.96 ± 0.02 (R² = 0.95) with a co-located anemometer. We show that quantification accuracy is largely insensitive to the choice of wind product (ERA5, IFS, or HRRR), an important robustness property for global operations. A residual underestimation at low emission rates, correlated with wind-model spatial resolution, is substantially reduced by a bias-correction approach combining a local background correction with an empirically recalibrated effective wind speed, which removes most of the residual bias without degrading accuracy at higher emission rates. Together, these results establish a transparent, statistically grounded baseline for the GHGSat constellation's detection and quantification performance and provide a methodological framework that can be extended as additional controlled-release data become available.
