b: Calibration and validation activities play a fundamental role in monitoring sensor performance, assessing image quality and building trust in Earth Observation products. Within the ΦSat-2 mission, these activities have recently focused on the characterization and mitigation of image degradations affecting the blue spectral band of the multispectral camera, first presented at VH-RODA 2025. Since then, significant efforts have been devoted to further characterizing the observed degradations and to developing and evaluating post-processing methods aimed at improving the quality of the delivered products.

The ΦSat-2 is a European Space Agency (ESA) 6U CubeSat launched on August 16, 2024. The mission carries a multispectral imager and an on-board AI framework running several AI applications. To overcome this situation, post processing methods dedicated to geometric and image quality improvement have been prototyped and evaluated. Also, for geometry, physical modelling and computer vision algorithms have been developed for absolute geolocation and inter band accuracy improvements. On the other hand, several image enhancement schemes including anti-aliasing, sharpening, de convolution algorithms have been set up (Wiener, Richardson-Lucy …)

In parallel, we are developing a dedicated Cal/Val dataset composed of radiometric, geometric, and spatial reference sites acquired by ΦSat-2. The dataset is designed to support the systematic evaluation of image quality metrics, including MTF, Point Spread Function (PSF), geometric accuracy, and spectral consistency, while providing benchmark data to the broader Earth Observation community with a view to developing open tools to fix common data quality issues. The initiative addresses the growing need for standardized datasets enabling reproducible assessment of onboard processing algorithms and AI-generated products. Furthermore, the collected reference acquisitions could be used to investigate AI-assisted approaches for the extraction of Cal/Val parameters, including robust estimation of MTF, PSF, and image cross-talk characteristics. These activities contribute to the emerging research area of "AI for Cal/Val", where traditional image quality metrics are exploited not only to characterize sensor performance but also to validate enhanced, reconstructed, compressed, or AI-generated EO products. Such capabilities are becoming increasingly relevant for future onboard intelligence systems and data certification frameworks.

Within this presentation, it is suggested to give an overview of proposed geometric and image enhancement algorithms and show data quality improvements depending on selected approach. The preliminary ΦSat-2 Cal/Val dataset is also presented as a benchmark to support the systematic characterization of the observed degradations and the quantitative assessment of the proposed correction and restoration methods. As the dataset is composed of native ΦSat-2 acquisitions, it preserves the sensor-specific image-quality issues observed in the mission data, including the degradations affecting the blue spectral band, thus providing a realistic basis for the evaluation of image quality and restoration techniques.

This presentation is an opportunity to discuss how Cal/Val algorithms and reference datasets can become assets not only for sensor characterization and validation, but also for image restoration purposes. Furthermore, these promising results open the discussion of porting such post-processing approaches on-board the platform as a value-added processing component to support AI processing.

b: A satellite calibration and validation (cal/val) site is being established in Sjökulla, Kirkkonummi, Finland (60.242 N, 24.383 E). b: Climate change is amplifying the frequency and intensity of wildfires, demanding faster and more reliable thermal Earth observation (EO) capabilities. OroraTech’s first operational constellation OTC-P1 provides data key to the detection and monitoring of wildfires with overpasses at 4am and 4pm; this represents the first step towards a goal of achieving 15-minute revisit times with an extended constellation to support efficient responses to rapidly evolving fire events. Central to this effort is our SAFIRE instrument, a compact and scalable class of thermal imagers based on uncooled microbolometers. b: The Moon has long been recognized as a highly stable radiometric reference source for the calibration and monitoring of Earth observation sensors. To support the increasing need for accurate and interoperable radiometric measurements across satellite missions, the LIME (Lunar Irradiance Model of ESA) model was developed, a physically based lunar irradiance model designed to provide SI-traceable predictions of disk-integrated lunar irradiance and reflectance.

LIME is derived from a multi-year record of ground-based lunar observations acquired at the Izaña Atmospheric Observatory and Teide Peak in Tenerife using a dedicated, SI-traceably calibrated lunar photometer. The model builds upon the analytical framework of the widely used ROLO model while incorporating a rigorous metrological approach, including uncertainty propagation from instrument calibration, measurement, atmospheric characterization, and model parameter estimation. Current model versions are based on hundreds of lunar irradiance observations collected over a broad range of lunar phases and libration conditions.

Recent developments significantly extend the capabilities and applicability of LIME. To support the needs of modern multispectral and hyperspectral satellite instruments, a spectral interpolation framework has been developed that combines the LIME reference wavelengths with high-resolution ASD lunar spectra, enabling irradiance predictions for arbitrary spectral response functions across an extended wavelength range. In addition, an initial implementation of lunar polarisation modelling has been introduced, providing estimates of the Degree of Linear Polarisation (DoLP) and Angle of Linear Polarisation (AoLP), with ongoing activities focused on validation and uncertainty characterisation. These developments are supported through the LIME Toolbox (LIME-TBX), an open-access software platform that enables simulation of lunar observations for ground-based and satellite instruments, supports user-defined spectral response functions, propagates model uncertainties, and provides outputs in formats suitable for calibration and validation applications.

This presentation provides an overview of the LIME project, including the measurement campaign, model development methodology, uncertainty framework, recent developments, and satellite validation activities. Comparisons against lunar observations from satellite sensors and existing lunar irradiance models demonstrate the performance of LIME and its suitability for absolute radiometric calibration and long-term monitoring applications.

b: The Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS) delivers geographical information on land cover, land use and their changes, ground motion, vegetation state, water cycle and surface energy variables for Europe and the whole globe. Particularly across the continent, Very High Resolution (VHR) space-borne imagery is one of the crucial inputs used for detection of fine details landscape elements delivered at very high scale.

CLMS relies on efficient and robust external validation frameworks to ensure the quality, consistency and alignment with users’ expectations of its diverse portfolio of land cover and land use products. In the absence of abundant, harmonized and independent thematic reference information at the continental scale in many cases, ground-based in-situ data and authoritative spatial information such as VHR and aerial imagery represents a critical source for high-quality, spatially-explicit sample interpretation and verification. While VHR products such as the European VHR mosaic and the Copernicus Contributing Missions support the production and validation of several CLMS products alike, authoritative national and regional orthoimagery accessed through the Copernicus Reference Data Access (CORDA) mechanism constitutes another valuable source of independent information for validation exercises.

This contribution presents the European CLMS validation framework and its experience in using CCM VHR imagery and authoritative aerial imagery for the validation of operationally produced datasets such as CLCplus Backbone, HRL-Grassland, HRL-Small Landscape Features or Urban Atlas. Within the CLMS validation framework, these resources provide the spatial detail and geometric fidelity required for sample interpretation, thematic accuracy assessment, plausibility checks, and quality control activities. Access through CORDA is an enabler of these activities.

The presentation will also discuss the use of reference data themselves and associated uncertainty. Although national orthophotos are generally considered authoritative datasets, differences in time stamps, access and quality introduce varying levels of uncertainty that should be explicitly accounted for in validation workflows. Finally, the presentation will outline recommendations for future improvements, including enhanced metadata on accuracy and lineage, more frequent updates, harmonised European specifications, improved transparency on uncertainty, and broader, easier access mechanisms to support next-generation CLMS portfolio and quality assurance of Earth observation products in general.

b: Future Earth Observation missions increasingly require radiometric measurements with improved absolute accuracy, long-term stability and traceability, particularly for climate applications where instrumental drifts can become comparable with the geophysical signals of interest.

QUASAR investigates an innovative onboard calibration concept based on correlated photon pairs generated by Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC), with the objective of establishing an intrinsically traceable reference for optical and near-infrared detectors. The approach exploits the Klyshko method for absolute quantum-efficiency calibration and its extension to high-flux imaging detectors through spatial correlations and Noise Reduction Factor (NRF) techniques, providing a possible route towards calibration of CCD, CMOS and SPAD-based instruments.
The project moves beyond the demonstration of the quantum-optics principle by assessing its potential advantage at Earth Observation instrument and product level.

The analysis links representative EO missions, detectors and spectral domains to quantitative performance metrics, including calibration uncertainty, long-term stability, sensitivity and traceability. Physical modelling and preliminary uncertainty budgets are used to identify the dominant contributions affecting the quantum calibration, including photon statistics, background and detector noise, mode mismatch, optical coupling, alignment, thermal effects and source stability.

These results are benchmarked against conventional calibration approaches and representative EO requirements, providing a quantitative assessment of the conditions under which a quantum reference could provide a meaningful improvement.

Particular attention is given to the propagation of calibration performance towards geophysical products, trying to identify where improved detector calibration can reduce the instrumental contribution to retrieval uncertainty and strengthen long-term climate records. At the same time, the analysis explicitly distinguishes detector-calibration improvements from uncertainties that remain dominated by atmospheric correction, angular response, scene heterogeneity and retrieval modelling.

The results provide a first quantitative framework for determining where quantum radiometric calibration can complement existing Cal/Val infrastructures and future reference missions, rather than replacing them. By combining quantum metrology, EO performance analysis and system-level considerations, QUASAR defines the performance conditions, technology constraints and potential integration scenarios required to progress from laboratory demonstrations towards a future onboard quantum calibration reference for next-generation Earth Observation missions.

b: With the recent momentum of open data movements, an ever-increasing volume of Earth Observation datasets has been made publicly available. This shift has significantly benefited international initiatives, such as the Terrain Mapping SubGroup (TMSG) under the Working Group on Calibration & Validation (WGCV) of the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) [1].

Following the foundational works of the Digital Elevation Model Intercomparison eXercise (DEMIX) [2]—which continues to establish standardized DEM terminology and assessment protocols using Very-High Resolution DEMs as reference data [3]—the TMSG proposed to host Ground Control Point Intercomparison eXercise (GCPIX) [4] activity.

The GCPs play a critical role in the geometric calibration, validation and registration of very high-resolution (VHR) optical, thermal, or radar Earth Observation (EO) missions. In this context, GCPIX aims to develop a harmonized, global Ground Control Point (GCP) database [5].

Currently, there is no platform dedicated to GCP visualization, query, GCP sharing and GCP management whilst many GCPs are available across different international agencies, space administrations, and research institutes, as discussed in [6]. Furthermore, there is no standard way to define a GCP and its usability.

Based on GCP match up database concept presented at VH RODA 2025 [7] [8], the GCP Viewer tool is now open to the community [9]. Also accessible from the CEOS Cal/Val portal [10], the GCP Viewer tool is an open-access web platform.

Geometric reference datasets acquired across European test fields, La Crau, Ankara, Piedmont and Grosseto, are available and several new datasets from heterogenous source of data (LIDAR, GRI) are planned to be integrated. Beside GCP sharing capability, the GCP Viewer platform is proposing agreed technical resources including methodological guidelines and protocols.

Our objective is to present the GCP Viewer platform and its functionalities in the context of the GCPIx activity. Therefore, one purpose is to discuss the proposed system, the technical trade off, the GCP ingestion / sharing process and the user interface. Another purpose is to report on collection status; referring to available reference dataset and foreseen evolutions. We strongly believe that this new tool will significantly simplify reference data provisioning for Cal/Val workflows. We also know that this long-term value strongly depends on the involvement of the community. In the last part, it is foreseen to open discussions on critical aspects of this initiative, namely provision of new dataset from community. b: C-CERT (Certified Calibration and Earth-observation Rating Tool) is an automated, sensor-agnostic data quality assessment tool built around a practical need: the Earth observation (EO) satellite data market needs an objective way to compare products based on how well they serve a specific use. For each delivered satellite data product, C-CERT runs a standards-traceable evaluation and returns an impartial quality rating, including a 0–100 score, an A–D grade, and a fitness-for-purpose verdict for each intended application. This gives government, institutional, and commercial users a shared certification standard that can keep pace with modern constellations and the volume of data they produce, beyond what traditional mission-by-mission calibration and validation can reasonably support.

The framework is organized around five diagnostic modules: data integrity, radiometric performance, spectral and channel consistency, spatial quality and stability, and information content. Each result is supported by pixel-level evidence, and every score is traceable to QA4EO, ISO 19157, and GUM. At the center of C-CERT is an SDI-developed radiative transfer model covering both optical and SAR observations. It provides a physics-based estimate of what a well-calibrated sensor should observe for a given scene, viewing geometry, and atmospheric state, giving the certification a first-principles reference rather than relying only on statistical comparison. C-CERT also uses tiered references, from internal consistency checks, to globally available reference missions, to surveyed calibration sites, so scenes anywhere on Earth can be certified with clear confidence in the evidence behind the grade.

C-CERT is designed to work at two scales. For a single scene, it issues a certificate for one delivered product. Across larger datasets, C-CERT is being developed to use the same modules to run in batch to characterize an archive, a constellation, or a multi-year time series. This broader view can reveal quality distributions, inter-sensor consistency, and calibration drift that may not be visible in any single scene.

We present the current development of C-CERT and discuss how a shared certification standard can help build trust across the EO supply chain. We also invite community discussion on certification schemes, reference tiers, and practical paths toward a common standard.

b: Air pollution, particularly concentrations of particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), continues to represent a significant threat to public health across Europe. To support environmental policies and regulatory actions, public authorities primarily depend on certified ground-based air quality monitoring networks. These systems provide the evidence required for decision-making processes, including the implementation of temporary traffic and emission reduction measures during pollution episodes. In Italy, monitoring activities are managed by the Regional and Provincial Environmental Protection Agencies (ARPA/APPA), coordinated nationally by ISPRA within the National System for Environmental Protection (SNPA), and aligned at the European level through the European Environment Agency (EEA) and the Joint Research Centre (JRC).

In parallel, satellite-based Earth Observation (EO) data are gaining recognition as an important complement to conventional in-situ monitoring. EO products can enhance spatial and temporal coverage, support urban and environmental planning, strengthen early warning capabilities, and improve public access to air quality information. Despite these advantages, satellite-derived data are not yet recognized as legally valid evidence for regulatory and enforcement purposes.
This presentation proposes a pathway toward the certification of EO-derived air quality data through:
Reviewing the existing certification framework governing surface-based air quality measurements;
Examining the associated regulatory, technical, and operational requirements;
Identifying key differences and gaps between current in-situ certification processes and EO-based observations;
Developing a phased roadmap, governance approach, and uncertainty assessment framework capable of extending certification principles to satellite products.

The work provides a comprehensive analysis of the current European regulatory framework for in-situ air quality monitoring and investigates how its fundamental principles could be adapted to Earth Observation data. Particular attention is given to the translation of regulatory requirements into practical operational procedures and quality assurance mechanisms.

The long-term objective is to facilitate the gradual incorporation of satellite-derived air quality information into official assessment frameworks and decision-support systems, thereby unlocking the full societal value of the rapidly growing Earth Observation sector.

b: Achieving both high spatial resolution and high radiometric accuracy is a prerequisite for the new generation of space borne optical instruments that serve climate research, Earth-system modelling, and defence applications. Building on long-standing expertise with multispectral imagers, CNES has broadened its competence to hyperspectral, thermal infrared (TIR), polarimetric payloads, and satellite swarms, adapting the processing chain to the specific physical characteristics of each case.

These emerging applications raise several challenges. New radiometric calibration techniques and models need to be developed, to take into account the specificities of a new spectral domain (e.g. TIR), light polarisation, high spectral resolution, or multiplatform sensors. This includes the physical models that help simulate or correct data, as well as the assessment of effects that are specific to sensor technology. Where appropriate, the methodology extends validated multispectral techniques (e.g., vicarious calibration using synthetic broadband composites) to generate reference products that can be cross-validated against legacy sensors.

Radiometric calibration and validation can employ several strategies, depending on the sensor, ranging from on-board calibration units (e.g. solar diffusers or internal black-bodies) to vicarious calibration, using well-characterised astronomical or terrestrial scenes, and dedicated instrumented sites.

For many years now, CNES has built a strong expertise in vicarious calibration methods, by assembling a multi decadal, homogeneous database of vicarious calibration data from a large number of optical sensors – including de-orbited sensors – enabling long-term stability of radiometric performances and statistically robust inter-sensor comparisons. This database, named SADE (Structure d’Accueil des Données d’Etalonnage, which is a French name for data repository for calibration measurements), is used with MUSCLE (MUlti Sensor CaLibration Environment), that implements calibration algorithms. A web based portal delivering calibration results based on SADE/MUSCLE will be released soon. CNES also operates historic VNIR-SWIR instrumented sites, takes part in RadCalNet, and is developing similar sites for the TIR domain and for hyperspectral needs. CNES is actively involved in the definition phase of space sensors, ensuring that the instrument specifications match user requirements, and developing the ground algorithms that process the image products. The associated studies can require airborne campaigns to generate representative data, thanks to hyperspectral bands and ultra-high resolution.

The presentation will give an overview of CNES activities related to image quality for the current and upcoming missions, to ensure that high resolution optical sensors meet the scientific and operational requirements of contemporary remote sensing programmes.

b: Satellite imagery and Earth Observation (EO) products are starting to be exposed to data manipulation, cyber threats and artificial intelligence (AI) generated data creating a need for methods to establish more trust in EO data and analytics. A way to make this harder to do is by layering multiple methods of validation, provenance and proof mechanisms to make it more costly both computationally and financially. This work explores new methods of proof mechanism and provenance metrics that exist in mobile devices and more traditional, non-edge, based computing to understand how authenticity, integrity, traceability and provenance can be improved when producing and validating EO data. Current proving mechanisms such as proof of location and time are especially interesting as translating these technologies from mobile devices to orbit would allow for exact satellite determination on their predictable orbital trajectories. Other proving methods such as proof of ownership, device identity, proof of humanity could also be used to isolate the location of EO datas creation. As well as these, with onboard analytic production, methods such as zero-knowledge machine learning could be used to generate proof that the analytics delivered to the ground are true while still not transmitting large datasets. With these layered proofs, EO observations could become more secure with the newest advances in cyber warfare, AI and misinformation.

b: The Ground Control Point Intercomparison eXercise (GCPIX) was initiated within the CEOS Working Group on Calibration and Validation (WGCV) to improve the availability, comparability and reuse of ground control information for geometric calibration and validation (Cal/Val). Initial GCPIX activities focused on the concept of a harmonised GCP resource, the clarification of terminology, quality and fitness-for-purpose criteria, and practical mechanisms for bringing existing reference collections together [1]. As the activity has progressed, however, it has become increasingly clear that the challenge extends beyond the availability of accurate GCP coordinates.

The rapidly growing diversity of EO sensors, spatial resolutions, wavelengths and acquisition geometries is accompanied by an equally diverse range of potential reference data, including surveyed points and targets, reference imagery and image chips, vector features, digital elevation and surface models, LiDAR and UAV point clouds, and SAR-derived references.

These resources are not directly interchangeable: their suitability depends on what physical feature or surface they represent, how that feature is observed by a particular sensor, how uncertainty is characterised, andwhetherthereferenceremainsvalidover time.Thisevolutionreinforcestheimportanceofinternational collaboration, since reliable geometric Cal/Val increasingly requires complementary expertise, reference resources and operational experience across space agencies, research and mapping institutions, commercial providers and Cal/Val practitioners.

This contribution provides an activity-status update and reports progress towards a common technical framework for geometric reference data. The GCPIX Technical Note has developed the initial conceptual tasks into a structured framework covering terminology and definitions, reference-data generation methodologies, uncertainty and traceability, metadata and reporting, interoperability, and representative Cal/Val applications. A key outcome is the treatment of a GCP not simply as an accurate coordinate, but as a documented reference entity linking an object-space definition with an image-space measurement. This distinction becomes particularly important in multi-sensor applications, where an optical feature, a radar scattering centre and a LiDAR or surface representation may correspond to related, but not necessarily identical, physical locations.

Beside, the GCPIX technical note became an asset to capture Cal / Val user requirements for designing an innovative GCP Visualization / Sharing platform: the GCP Viewer tool [2] Our first objective is to present a status on GCPIX activities showing progression from the initial concept of a shared GCP database towards a broader, federated geometric reference-data framework, as defined in the related technical note.

Our second objective is to present GCPViewer platform and its functionalities in the context of the GCPIX activities. One purpose will be to discuss the proposed system, the technical trade off, the GCP ingestion / sharing process and the user interface. A second purpose will be to report on collection status; referring to available reference dataset and foreseen evolutions.
